title: Easton forfeits boys' game to Cambridge-SD
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Easton forfeits boys' game to Cambridge-SD

 January 10, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 721
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Easton High's boys' basketball team has forfeited its game Thursday at Cambridge-South Dorchester.Thursday's girls' game between the two schools will be played as scheduled at Easton High at 4 p.m., but spectators will not be allowed to attend.
The decision to forfeit the boys' game and play the girls' game without spectators is largely connected to the Oct. 27 football game between the two schools at Easton High that was stopped with just under 7 minutes remaining in the third quarter because of altercations away from the playing field.
At that game, the Easton and Cambridge-SD coaching staffs led their teams off the field while fans were instructed to leave the stadium by school administrators and local law enforcement officers. Three teenagers were arrested following the altercations.
The pattern that is emerging — basketball games scheduled between the two schools at Easton High this season will be played without fans; basketball games slated for Cambridge-SD will be forfeited by Easton High. The issue came down to playing the game with limited spectators. Easton wanted to limit or play without spectators. Cambridge-SD wanted spectators allowed.
This past Sunday, Easton High announced on its Instagram page, "Due to events that occurred during the EHS vs. CSD football game in the Fall, we have decided not to allow spectators at our upcoming girls and boys basketball game against CSD at Easton High School. As always, safety is a top priority. We apologize for any inconvenience and thank you for your support and understanding."
On Tuesday, the administrative offices of Cambridge-South Dorchester posted a statement on its Facebook page announcing Easton's decision to forfeit Thursday's boys' game at Cambridge-SD, and the Feb. 15 girls' game slated at Cambridge-SD.
"It is with great disappointment that we must convey this news: Easton High School has decided to forfeit the upcoming girls' and boys' basketball games scheduled to be held at Cambridge South Dorchester High School on Jan. 11 and Feb. 15," the statement said. "This decision was made by Easton High School and was not influenced by Cambridge-South Dorchester High in any way."
The post went on to say, "As a result of Easton High School's prearranged decision to forfeit these games, Cambridge South Dorchester High School will be credited with the wins for both of the boys' and girls' teams. We regret that parents, spectators and community members will not have the opportunity to witness these anticipated games.
"While we extend our best wishes to Easton High School, it is essential to emphasize that safety remains our top priority. We too understand the importance of maintaining a safe and secure environment for all involved.
Cambridge-SD High School was closed Wednesday due to weather conditions. Phone calls to the office of Cambridge-SD athletic director Casey O'Bier went unanswered.
On Wednesday, Talbot County Public Schools released a second statement in an email, saying that following the football game, administrators talked with coaches, athletes and parents about safety at future events.
"TCPS made the difficult decision not to allow spectators at upcoming home basketball events against CSD," the statement read.
Home games against Cambridge-SD will be livestreamed.
The statement continued that Talbot County school administrators asked that Cambridge-SD limit spectators at their home games.
"They chose not to," according to the Talbot County schools statement.
"Because the safety of our students and staff is always our highest priority, we have decided not to travel to CSD for the boys' and girls' basketball games on Jan. 11 and Feb. 15, thereby forfeiting those games," the statement read. "We value our relationship with our Dorchester County neighbors and believe this decision is in the best interests of all of the athletes involved."
The Easton and Cambridge-SD rivalry is one of the Bayside Conference's richest, especially in football and boys' basketball.
Entering Thursday's boys contest, Cambridge-SD (7-0 overall) was sitting atop the North Bayside with a 6-0 record and bidding for its first division title since 2020. Following the Vikings are second-place Queen Anne's (6-1) and Easton (5-1). Thursday's forfeit moves the Vikings to 8-0 overall and 7-0 in the division, while Easton slips to 6-4 overall, 5-2 division.
The boys' game at Easton is scheduled for Feb. 15 and will not have spectators.
Cambridge-SD's girls enter today's game at 5-2 overall, 4-2 North, trailing division leaders Queen Anne's (7-0, 6-0) and Kent Island (6-1, 6-0). Easton's girls are currently 3-6, 3-3.
Star Democrat Reporter Natalie Jones contributed to this article.

title: LIONS PIN DOWN HISTORY
author: Bill Haufe
content:
LIONS PIN DOWN HISTORY

 January 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 981
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — John Waters, Queen Anne's County High's girls head wrestling coach, wondered if his team recognized it was wrestling with history.Then again, maybe Queen Anne's was more focused on just winning than getting its name in the record books.
The Lions got both Friday night, stringing together five consecutive pinfalls before Kaylynn Bryant delivered a first-period fall in the second-to-last match that clinched Queen Anne's 48-36 victory over Winters Mill in the first girls dual match in the history of the Maryland Public Secondary Schools Athletic Association, where all 14 weight classes competed without a forfeit.
"I don't think they realized the magnitude of the match; that Winters Mill was one of the first true girls teams," Waters said of his team. "They don't forfeit weight classes."
On this night, neither did Queen Anne's.
"They come in every day; they work," Waters said of his team. "And it's just like, 'OK, cool. It's time to wrestle.' I'm extremely proud of them."
Winters Mill defeated Queen Anne's a year ago in a dual meet in Centreville. The two met again in the finals of Maverick Duals at Manchester Valley in December, with Queen Anne's earning a 48-36 victory — the same score as Friday — ending the Falcons' two-year win streak.
Friday's third clash had the early markings of another close finish.
Queen Anne's Annalise Michael — one of seven first-year wrestlers in the Lions' starting lineup Friday — rallied from a 12-5 deficit to pin Nijae Tate in 4:21 of the 100-pound match.
"Started out with Annalise; that was a big swing match that we won," Waters said. "She fought off her back a couple of times and ended up getting the pin. I think that provided a lot of energy for the girls and they fed off it."
Winters Mill tied the match 6-all at 105, Alexa Hresko earning a first-period fall over Celeste Molina. Queen Anne's needed just 1:19 to move back in front, when Ally Conley, who won a state title in 2022, caught Carli Ireland in a headlock and hit a throw for a fall at 110. The Falcons again answered, as Christina Padilla (115) pinned Bevyn Branham in 1:03.
The Lions then reeled off five consecutive pins to build a commanding 30-point cushion.
Bree Conard — granddaughter of Hall of Fame coach Dan Zottarelli, who guided Kent County High's boys to back-to-back 2A-1A state titles in 2001-02, and was in attendance Friday — was taken down in the first period, but worked off bottom to register a fall in 2:28 over Jayla Shropshire at 120, giving the Lions a lead they never relinquished at 18-12.
Finley Patchett (125), another first-year wrestler, rolled Taylor Scholl to her back for a pin in 1:22. Queen Anne's Delaney Gray followed suit at 130, pinning Hailee Smith in 1:21 for a 30-12 lead. Linda Vail continued the roll, with a fall over Maggie Morley in 3:38 of the 135-pound match. Winters Mill's Kayla Goodwin (140) looked ready to end that streak, when she built a 4-1 lead on Keira Corcoran in the first period. But Corcoran scored an early reverse in the second en route to pinning Goodwin in 3:22.
"Tonight we got the matchups that we wanted and they were better," said Winters Mill head coach John Lowe, a St. Michaels High graduate who coached Waters at McDaniel College from 1997-99. "All props to coach Waters. He does a great job."
But Waters, who won a state title at 103 pounds for Queen Anne's in 1996, deflected any credit afterwards.
"I'm happy for all the girls," Waters said. "I'm extremely happy for (boys head) coach (Dave) Stricker. I just sat in the corner. If it wasn't for coach Stricker and his vision a couple of years ago, we wouldn't have the girls team.
"It just so happened that he's coaching one team and we needed a coach for the other team," Waters continued. "This is a team effort. I'm just one of the coaches. We have several coaches that are at practice every day that help these girls, and boys, wrestle. It's great for the program."
Winters Mill ended the Lions' run at 145, when Kimora Harrid pinned Lilly Hammond in the first period, and began whittling away at its deficit. The Falcons' Gabbie McLeod followed with a first-period fall over Morgan Morris at 155. Maiah Sweet (165) moved Winters Mill within 42-30 with a first-period pin of Addie Dickens.
The Falcons had a chance to draw even with two matches remaining, but those hopes ended when Bryant pinned Morgan Tolle with 7 seconds remaining in the first period of the 190-pound match, pushing the Lions' lead to 48-30.
"We had a couple of girls, they got their first varsity matches tonight and stepped in for some girls that were injured, and some that were sick," Waters said. "To not have our true lineup and to come in and do what we did. … Pretty impressive. I give all the credit to the girls."
Winters Mill's Jade Love (235) capped the match with a first-period pin of Maggie Rooney.
"They won it tonight. But we're going to focus on March now," Lowe said in reference to this year's state tournament, where a girls' team champion will be crowned for the first time in MPSSAA history. "We've got some stuff to work on before March."
Stricker, who watched his boys team defeat Winters Mill, 42-34, before losing to Southern of Anne Arundel, 42-33, snuck a couple glances at the girls match between the two boys dual bouts.
"We're probably the two biggest teams in the state of Maryland," Stricker said of Queen Anne's and Winters Mill, who figure to get competition from Francis Scott Key, La Plata and Manchester Valley at the state tournament. "To go toe-to-toe three times (with Winters Mill), it's what you want to grow the sport. They're exciting matches. Hope we can convince somebody up top that we can have a girls state duals at some point."

title: KINGS AND QUEENS
author: Bill Haufe
content:
KINGS AND QUEENS

 January 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 1226
 Words 

 Read News Document

 SNOW HILL — It was a first for Cambridge-South Dorchester High's boys track program and head coach Clint Falduto.But it was the last conference indoor title run for Kent Island's girls team, at least under head coach Justin Holland.
Tori Willis Jr., won two individual titles to lead the Vikings to their first boys team crown indoors in school history, and Gabrielle Bernhard struck gold twice and set a new standard Wednesday, pacing the Buccaneers to their fifth girls title in six years during the Bayside Conference indoor track and field championships at the Worcester County Recreation Center.
"I was nervous," said Holland of the girls' competition, which ended with Kent Island totaling 96½ points — 23 ahead of runner-up Parkside.
Holland, who is set to retire from coaching after this season, had reason to be nervous.
Historically a power in the middle- and long-distance events, the Bucs did not score a point in the 1,600 or 3,200 meters Wednesday, had Kaitlyn Stevens place fifth for their only points in the 800, and were an uncharacteristic fifth in the 4x800 relay.
"This is not the stereotypical Kent Island track team," Holland said. "The four-by-eight (relay), I can't remember us not either winning, or you know, (placing) top three in the four-by-eight. I'm not used to this.
"And then when it comes to the (800), that's when we usually win the meet," Holland continued. "It's tight and then we go to the 800 and we triple score in the eight, and we seal the deal, because everybody knows we're going to be in the top four in the four-by-four relay. It was interesting."
Bernhard helped make up for those rare deficiencies, leading a 1-2-4 finish in both the 500 meters and pole vault.
"I'm happy that she switched over from cheerleading to track," Holland said of Bernhard, who did cheer and ran indoors last year, but is running track only this year.
Like many of Wednesday's competitors, Bernhard ran all her events in a fairly tight time frame. She placed second to Cambridge-SD's Enazajah Young (8.76 seconds) in the 55 hurdles, clocking a 9.03. She came right back and took fourth (45.26) in the 300. Two events later, she was back on the track, running the 500.
"Last year she was in the four-by-two (relay), but I had to drop her all the time because the four-by-two and the pole vault were all in the same (time) spot," Holland said. "So this year she's been scoring individually in the three and the five. And she wasn't a 500 runner. But she ran cross country this year so she knew she was in shape. So I said, 'Let's try the 500.' Of course that's the one she won."
But it took some doing, as she rallied past sophomore teammate Reece Heyliger over the final 50 meters to win in 1:24.59. Heyliger, who overcame a false start in the 55 to run strong legs for the second-place 4x200 relay and first-place 4x400 relay, was second in 1:24.78, followed by teammate Siena Koch (1:27.66) in fourth.
Bernhard, who early in the season broke Fiona Mulligan's school indoor pole vault record when she cleared 11 feet, 1 inch, capped her day by winning the pole vault with a new conference record effort of 11-2. The senior was followed by teammates Siena Koch (8 foot) in second and Nora Koch (6-6) in fourth.
Parkside (1:53.95) won the 4x200, but Kent Island's team of Kendra Coffey, Siena Koch, Heyliger and Seryna Stephan was second in 1:57.12. The Bucs punctuated the ninth girls indoor championship of Holland's career in the 4x400 relay, as Heyliger, Coffey, Stephan and Stevens won in 4:31.45.
The defending Class 1A state champion in the girls 55 meters, Cambridge-SD's Young held off Parkside's RaNiya Corbin (7.56) to win the conference crown in 7.45, before coming back to win the 55 hurdles in 8.76.
"Enazajah is a talent that's hard to match," Falduto said. "She's just incredibly athletic. We're trying to build her stamina up for some more different events other than the short ones. This could be a great opportunity for her future after high school. Just excited to see how she continues to control this season."
Falduto was excited to see what his boys team could do this season, and Wednesday the Vikings showed why, rolling to their first Bayside title indoors with 134½ points — 74 points ahead of runner-up Kent Island.
"They're stacked," Holland said of Cambridge-SD.
At the top of that stack is Willis, who started his day by winning the 55 meters in 6.576 — nipping Parkside's Nasir Bolden (6.578) — then leading a 1-2-3 Vikings sweep in the 55 hurdles. Willis took gold in 8.07 seconds followed by teammates Antonio Blueford (second, 8.121) and Jaydene Smith (third, 8.129).
"We've been training Tori to prepare for a day like this, knowing that come the state meet it would not be a similar type (of situation)," Falduto said in reference to the tight time schedule. "We knew coming into the Bayside meet and the competition we had, that he had a great opportunity to be a medalist in all four events."
A junior, Willis placed second in the 300 (37.10) to Snow Hill's Logan Hurney (36.88) before closing his day with a third-place in the 500 (1:13.71), completing a 34-point day.
Competing indoors for the first time, sophomore Majestic Jones gave Cambridge-SD an added boost, winning the high jump with a leap of 5-10.
Then there was Viking junior Tekai Drummond, who logged runner-up finishes in the 1,600 (4:55.50), 3,200 (10:49.39) and 800 (2:09.11), and ran a leg on the third-place 4x400 relay.
"Tekai has been probably the backbone of our team," Falduto said. "He was a sprinter last year, rarely did an 800 here or there, but as he's moved now to the mile, two mile. What he has done has really changed the dynamics of our team.
"We had a goal set on having a championship year," Faldutot said of his boys team. "Starting off the postseason with the indoor Bayside championship is a huge success for our team, and where they're at, and where they're heading. We had a goal set and we accomplished it for the boys. Everybody showed up in my opinion so I was very excited about that."
Queen Anne's County junior Ben Marks looks comfortable and in command en route to winning the boys 1,600 meters (4:51.13) and 800 (2:03.25).
"We didn't want him to run too hard," Queen Anne's head coach Natasha Dawson said of Marks, who's been focusing on the 1,600 this indoor season. "He hasn't run the 800 competitively this season. So we needed to make sure he got a good time so that sets him up for a good heat in regions."
Easton's Jed Smith led from start to finish in the boys 3,200. The senior began widening his lead with six laps remaining and won in 10:41.28. Smith joined Colin Smith, Jacob Camper and William Orndoff to give the Warriors victory in the boys 4x800 relay (8:49.39).
The Warriors got a second individual champion, as senior Sumayah Wilkins won the high jump, clearing the bar at 5 feet. Easton's Marvin Foster was second in the boys shot put (42-10½).
North Caroline junior Morgan Knott outdueled Snow Hill's Allie Suarezapecheche to win the girls 800 in 2:36.43. Knott also teamed with sophomores Seanna Rupp, Reece Bisesi and Linda Ridgell for victory in the 4x800 relay (10:49.95). Ridgell was runner-up in the 3,200 (12:46.96).

title: Clark, Iowa drawing sold-out crowds even on the road
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Clark, Iowa drawing sold-out crowds even on the road

 February 1, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 887
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Caitlin Clark has been a must-see attraction all season, with sold-out arenas where some tickets have gone for thousands of dollars on the secondary market.The prices are only expected to go higher as the Iowa star approaches the NCAA all-time scoring record over the next few weeks.
While teams like Tennessee and UConn would draw huge crowds on the road in the past and South Carolina has had a strong fan base the last few years, Clark is different. There has never been anything like it in women's basketball when an individual player has drawn so much interest from fans wanting to see her play.
"Nobody's ever had a player like this. She's a combination of Pete Maravich and Steph Curry," said Fox announcer Gus Johnson. "She plays in a different dimension and realm. Her ability to see, understand and anticipate the game and then from a physical aspect shoot the ball from almost anywhere when she gets into the frontcourt. Not even Diana Taurasi had this kind of range."
Schools that have hosted Iowa have seen an attendance increase over 150% compared to their other home games on average. Northwestern had the first sellout in school history on Wednesday night when Clark and Iowa came to visit.
According to ticket marketplace Vivid Seats, the top five most in-demand NCAA women's games this year have featured Iowa. The average price of tickets for the Hawkeyes since Clark joined the team in 2020 is up 224% and the average distance traveled by a fan to watch Iowa play is up 34% from last season.
"It's honestly, hard for me to wrap my head around. It's crazy, it's crazy the way people scream my name and really support us and I try to make time for as many as them as I can," Clark said. "Like whenever I walk off the court, it's so special just the way people scream our names and are so excited for our team. And that's something that never gets old. I was that kid a few years back, so it's crazy how time flies and I just try to soak it all in, every single moment."
It's not just kids who want to see Clark and her deep 3's in action.
Former Iowa high school teammates Susan Johnstad, Deb Littlefield and Stephanie Fournier met at the Iowa-Rutgers game on Jan. 5 in Piscataway, New Jersey. They played basketball and softball together at Roland Story High School, about 45 miles from where Clark grew up in Des Moines.
"It's been 30 years since we've all been together," said Johnstad, who suggested they travel from their current homes in Virginia, Massachusetts and Iowa to watch Clark. "We played six-on-six basketball, and Iowa has such a tradition of supporting women's basketball. Clark's skill set is just amazing. In her recent commercial for Gatorade, she said she dreams big — and it shows."
Johnstad says she's proud to see the joy last year's AP player of the year brings to fans wearing her No. 22 jersey, young and old.
"I'm a fan girl, for sure," said Johnstad, who is an administrator at Virginia Tech. "I can see her play on television. But (it's fun) to be able to see the people lined up beforehand and the girls working on their signs and doing the face paints."
Clark is part of a new generation of stars that fans can easily and constantly see, through highlights on social media and games available on a whole host of networks and streaming services.
Back when Candace Parker, Diana Taurasi, Maya Moore and Sheryl Swoopes were dominating the game it was harder to see them play. Twitter and Instagram weren't around — YouTube was launched in 2005 — and players weren't allowed to star in national commercial campaigns like Clark is doing with State Farm and Nike.
Last year's national championship game that featured Iowa and LSU drew almost 10 million viewers. This year, the Hawkeyes have already had games on NBC, Fox and ESPN. The overtime loss to Ohio State on NBC averaged 1.93 million viewers across the network and Peacock, peaking at 3.9 million during overtime. Over a million fans tuned in for Iowa's win over Indiana on Fox.
Also in that crowd for the game at Rutgers was New Jersey Devils President Jake Reynolds. With him were his three daughters, Makenzie, 13, Katelyn, 10, and Harper, 8.
"This is something we decided to go to. Not a Rutgers season ticket holder, but this was part of the Caitlin Clark phenomenon," he said. "It was something that I sat there in amazement, just looking at the energy of what was going on around this event. Then I was blown away by just the response from so many fans. And then I was really proud to see so many young girls there."
Reynolds said watching Clark play in person has had a lasting effect on his daughters.
"To be able to, one, just witness the phenomenon that it is," he said. "To be able to give my girls the opportunity and the experience to see that firsthand, someone that inspires them and someone that they aspire to be like, to be able to give them that experience and be able to share that experience with them is something that here we are several weeks later and it is still something that is talked about in our house."

title: SEEING DOUBLE
author: Bill Haufe
content:
SEEING DOUBLE

 February 7, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 851
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — Katie Murphy has seen it all season."They tried to shut Morgan (Quade) down. They tried to shut Avery (McCall) down," Saints Peter and Paul High's girls head basketball coach said of Worcester Prep trying to clamp down on her top two leading scorers. "We needed everybody to step up and Lucy did it."
Sophomore Lucy Rankin stepped up like never before Wednesday, notching a career-high 16 points to go with 10 rebounds for her first-ever double-double, as the Sabres romped to a 49-15 victory over Worcester Prep in an Eastern Shore Independent Athletic Conference clash on senior night.
"She really stepped up, 'cause when that stuff happens we need the other three (starters) to step up," Quade said of Rankin. "She did really good with that tonight."
Rankin hit two free throws to give the Sabres their first points and a 2-2 tie, scored a layup midway through the first quarter to give Sts. Peter & Paul a lead it steadily widened, then made another foul shot to cap a 17-5 first quarter for the home team.
"Our coaches told us that this would happen," said Rankin of the Mallards trying to limit Quade and McCall. "So they said I needed to step up and move the ball and drive to the basket more. Once I started to get more comfortable I loosened up a bit and started to just go with the flow. This is a surprise to me."
Rankin scored on a layup and a put-back as the Sabres outscored Worcester, 15-0, in the second quarter to take a commanding 32-5 lead into the locker room.
"She really came through," Murphy said of Rankin, who had nine first-half points. "And everybody played the role they needed to play today."
One night after losing to ESIAC rival Delmarva Christian by 10, the Sabres cranked up the defensive pressure on Worcester early in the first quarter. Sts. Peter & Paul pressed Worcester full court, creating multiple turnovers while holding the Mallards scoreless the final 14 minutes of the first half.
"We've been fine tuning the press and changing different roles and different positions, and making sure that they're cutting off that middle person," Murphy said. "They did it pretty well today. And they were jumping for balls and getting the steals."
Despite Worcester's defensive efforts, Quade and McCall each finished in double figures. Quade, the Sabres' lone senior, finished with 14 points, eight rebounds and six steals. A sophomore, McCall scored all 12 of her points in the first half, and totaled four rebounds, three steals and three blocked shots.
Worcester ended an 18-plus minute scoring drought with just under 4 minutes remaining in the third quarter, and matched the Sabres in scoring during a 7-7 third. But Sts. Peter & Paul continued to play solid half-court defense in the fourth, limiting the visitors to just one basket from the field — that coming with 4 minutes left when Sydney Mize hit a 3-pointer.
"I think today we moved the ball quicker," said Quade, comparing the Sabres' loss Tuesday to Delmarva Christian to Wednesday's rout. "I think that's what kind of killed us last night. They were trapping us and we weren't moving it fast enough to get it around their traps, and if we did we would have found the open person really easily. Today I think we definitely moved it better. And honestly with them taking me and Avery out it kind of opened it up for the other three (Rankin, Sam Murphy and Annie Albright)."
With another potential showdown with Delmarva Christian in the playoffs looming, Coach Murphy was pleased with how her team rebounded from Tuesday's loss.
"Our defense is doing very well right now," Murphy said. "Every ball is a Sabre ball. They are supposed to go after it. I'm very happy with our underclassmen because they took the lead from our starters and they were after every ball, causing a bunch of jump balls. It's probably the most jump balls we've had in a game so far. Boxing out, rebounding, looking for the open player, making sure everybody was covered, they also did very well."
KENT ISLAND 39 STEPHEN DECATUR 33
BERLIN — Sydney Riska had 13 points and 15 rebounds Wednesday, leading the Buccaneers past the Seahawks.
Makayla Kropfelder added 10 points for Kent Island.
BOYS BASKETBALL
SSPP 72 WORCESTER PREP — Robbie Cunningham had 17 points and JJ Rardin 16 Wednesday, as the Sabres rolled past the Mallards.
On Tuesday, Braydan Smith drilled eight 3-pointers for a 24-point effort, leading Saints Peter & Paul to a 62-53 victory over Key School in a Maryland Interscholastic Athletic Association C Conference game. Garett Hemingway finished with 18.
QUEEN ANNE'S 65 NORTH DORCHESTER 41
CENTREVILLE — Vince Gilberto scored 16 points to eclipse the 1,000-point mark for his career Tuesday while pacing the Lions past the Eagles.
Jimmy Holthaus had 11 for Queen Anne's County.
COLONEL 80 KENT COUNTY 70
WORTON — Dreden Lake scored 29 points Tuesday, leading the Colonels.
Jazir Dickerson had 22 points and Makiah Batson finished with 20 for Colonel Richardson.
Jysir Valentine led the Trojans with 20 points. Larry Steward had 14 for Kent County, and Dwah Harris and Jonah Somerville each had 13.

title: DELAY OF GAME
author: Bill Haufe
content:
DELAY OF GAME

 February 8, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 856
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Domonique Foxworth played his first organized tackle football game at 10 years old.Now Foxworth has a son who turns 11 on Super Bowl Sunday who wants to play tackle. Foxworth won't allow it. His son is playing flag football instead.
When might he allow his son to play tackle? Foxworth said, "We'll see."
"It's definitely not going to be before high school," said Foxworth, a former NFL cornerback and former president of the NFL Players Association. "I guess that would be the first time that we even consider the conversation. Right now he's in the fifth grade, so we've got some time for him to fall in love with something else."
Interviews with several former NFL players, some of whom played tackle football before high school, revealed a range of opinions about whether children should participate in tackle leagues.
Some are categorically opposed to youth playing tackle before age 12 or 14. Others said they would consider what a child wanted. All interviewed for this article said their thoughts about the sport had evolved since their days as youth players.
"I honestly don't see the benefit of playing tackle football at a young age because flag football now is so available," said Muhammad Oliver, a former defensive back who played four years in the NFL.
Oliver said if taught correctly the skills learned in flag football can translate to tackle football. He said flag football allows kids to pick up the fundamentals of the sport and understand how it's played.
Oliver has seven children, four of whom are boys ages 27, 23, 12 and 9. His oldest son, Isaiah, plays for the San Francisco 49ers. Oliver allowed Isaiah to begin playing in a tackle league at age 8. If he had it to do over again, he said, Isaiah wouldn't have played tackle football until he was 12.
Oliver said his experience as a youth tackle football coach and as president of NX Level AthletX, a youth multisport development program in Goodyear, Arizona, has influenced his thinking. So has recent medical research linking youth tackle football to later-life challenges, such as impulse control and cognitive decline.
"With all the information now about concussions and how often concussions are happening and the number of concussions that players have had over their lifetime, I just don't feel like the contact is necessary young," Oliver said.
Former Super Bowl champion and Hall of Fame linebacker Harry Carson has been outspoken in warning of the risks of brain injury from the sport.
In 2018, Carson was one of the ex-players to appear at a news conference sponsored by the Concussion Legacy Foundation announcing a campaign to discourage tackle football before the age of 14. Carson has repeatedly said in interviews that if he had it to do again, he would not have played football.
Neither of Carson's two sons played football at a competitive level, he said. Carson, who played 13 seasons for the New York Giants, has discouraged his grandson from playing.
Carson advocates for transparency and education. "I would like for the surgeon general to issue a warning to parents," he said, adding that adults should understand the risks of the sport.
"Every parent should sign a waiver to fully understand what they are signing their kids up for when they play football or a contact sport," Carson said.
"Most parents of little boys of color will continue to allow their kids to play," Carson said, "because, you know, they don't want to deny their kids the opportunity to play because he has talent … not fully understanding that their kids may suffer the consequences down the road."
That differs somewhat from the view of Bruce Harper, a former New York Jets running back and kick returner whose NFL career lasted from 1977 to 1984. Harper never had to face a parental decision about youth football. He has two daughters, neither of whom played the sport.
However, Harper said the decision should be left to the child.
"It's a decision each kid individually has to make. I don't think the parents should decide for the kid if they can play or not," he said.
The NFLPA has no formal policy regarding tackle football for kids. However, the players union has backed several youth initiatives including both tackle and flag football. The players union also supports members serving on the boards of USA Football and other youth leagues. Additionally, the union provides financial and community support to players running football camps for kids, but these camps primarily stay away from tackle.
"We encourage every level of football … to implement the health and safety protocols we have at the NFL level," said George Atallah, the NFLPA's assistant executive director of external affairs. "We don't have a specific position on when we think young people should play it. That's for the medical experts to determine."
Foxworth, who played for three teams from 2005-2011, sustained many injuries throughout his career. He's been able to deal with injuries to his body, but brain injury will always be something he's mindful of.
"I still wouldn't trade it for the life that I've had access to," Foxworth said of his football career. "But it's all a different conversation when you start talking about your brain."

title: Gunston School crew set to join WMIRA
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Gunston School crew set to join WMIRA

 February 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 271
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — The Gunston School will join the Washington Metropolitan Interscholastic Rowing Association (WMIRA), the region's premier rowing conference, this spring.While Gunston has regularly competed against WMIRA teams at national regattas like Head of the Schuylkill in Philadelphia, the school is now eligible to compete in the conference championship regatta on May 5.
"Each year our students and coaches continue to elevate the quality and competitiveness of the program," Head of School John Lewis said, "and we're eager to join the ranks of the best public and private school rowing teams in our area. We're grateful that the WMIRA expanded its geographical reach to include us, and we look forward to welcoming these teams to home regattas at Gunston."
The WMIRA includes independent and parochial school teams like DeMatha, Georgetown Day School, St. Albans, Gonzaga, Holton Arms, and National Cathedral School, as well as Montgomery County public school powerhouses such as Blair, Bethesda-Chevy Chase, Walter Johnson, and Walt Whitman.
"I'm proud of our rowers, and appreciative of the WMIRA," said Natalie Reading, Gunston's head crew coach and assistant athletic director for waterfront athletics. "This opportunity not only enhances the competitiveness of Gunston's rowing team but also opens doors to a broader range of experiences and challenges. We aim to continue to build on our 2023 Maryland State championship performance."
In addition to the WMIRA, Gunston will again host the Maryland State rowing championship on Saturday, April 27, on its 75-acre campus on the Corsica River. Spectators are invited to bring chairs and/or blankets and watch the 1,500-meter sprint style race with 4's and 8's, men and women's varsity, junior varsity and novice event categories.

title: Terps coaching great Driesell dies
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Terps coaching great Driesell dies

 February 17, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 1514
 Words 

 Read News Document

 COLLEGE PARK — Lefty Driesell, the Hall of Fame coach whose folksy drawl belied a fiery on-court demeanor that put Maryland on the college basketball map and enabled him to rebuild several struggling programs, died Saturday. He was 92.Driesell died at his home in Virginia Beach, Virginia, his family said.
Maryland honored Driesell with a moment of silence before its game against No. 14 Illinois Saturday. The team wore throwback uniforms from the 1970s previously worn on Jan. 21, when the Terrapins honored Driesell with an "Ode to Lefty."
Driesell finished with 786 victories over parts of five decades and was the first coach to win more than 100 games at four NCAA Division I schools. He started at Davidson in 1960 before bringing Maryland into national prominence from 1969-86, a stay that ended with the cocaine-induced death of All-American Len Bias.
Driesell then won five regular-season conference titles over nine seasons at James Madison and finished with a successful run at Georgia State from 1997 to 2003.
"His contributions to the game go way beyond wins and losses, and he won a lot," former Duke coach Mike Krzyzewski said after Driesell finally made the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in 2018. "It's an honor he's deserved for a long time."
Driesell launched the college basketball tradition known as Midnight Madness on Oct. 15, 1971. At three minutes after midnight on the first day of practice as sanctioned by the NCAA, Driesell had his players take a mandatory mile run on the track inside the Maryland football stadium.
The lighting was provided by the headlights of a few cars parked at one end of the stadium. The motivation came from Driesell's prodding and the estimated 800 students who gathered to watch the unpublicized event.
"I've done a lot of crazy things to get attention, but that wasn't one of them," Driesell said years later. "I was just trying to get an early jump on practice. I had no idea what it was going to lead to."
Driesell also helped knock down racial barriers in the college game. He made George Raveling the first Black coach in the Atlantic Coast Conference by hiring him as an assistant in 1969. Driesell's effort to recruit Charlie Scott to play at Davidson helped make the future NBA star become the first African American scholarship athlete to attend North Carolina.
Scott initially committed to Davidson before choosing UNC but acknowledged that Driesell paved the way.
"I think if there had never been a Lefty Driesell, there would never have been a Charlie Scott attending North Carolina," said Scott, who joined the Hall of Fame in 2018 with Driesell. "My commitment to go to Davidson really opened up all the other schools in the recruiting process."
Race played no factor in Driesell's effort to recruit the best players.
"He did so many great things in marketing the game and opened up so many doors for many African Americans players and coaches like myself," said Len Elmore, who played for Driesell at Maryland from 1971-74. "Lefty was a trailblazer and an innovator."
Walking onto the court at Maryland to the tune of "Hail to the Chief," Driesell would thrust both arms in the air — two fingers extended on each hand with the V for victory sign — amid a standing ovation. On the sideline, he would often stomp his foot to show his displeasure with a call, and if things got really intense he would peel off his sports jacket, toss it to the floor and trample it.
Yet, Driesell rarely raised his voice off the court and had a knack for charming the parents of potential recruits with an assuring, homespun style that smacked of his Southern roots.
"He had a big personality, was an excellent recruiter and he helped put Maryland basketball on the map," said Brad Davis, a guard at Maryland from 1974-77 before heading to the NBA.
Driesell was inducted into the College Basketball Hall of Fame in 2007, but his entry into the Naismith shrine proved more elusive. He was a finalist four times before receiving the necessary 75% vote three months after his 86th birthday. The long snub, many speculated, came because Driesell was forced to resign at Maryland in 1986 after Bias overdosed on cocaine in a campus dorm after being drafted by the Boston Celtics.
Maryland had to pay Driesell for the rest of his 10-year contract because it could find no wrongdoing on his part. But his departure meant Driesell never got to fulfill the declaration he made upon taking over in College Park — he would make Maryland the "UCLA of the East."
Under Driesell, the Terrapins didn't enjoy the success John Wooden had at UCLA. Maryland failed to reach the Final Four during his 17-year stay, but the Terps won or shared five ACC regular-season titles and captured the league tournament in 1984 — on Driesell's fifth trip to the final.
Looking back on his "UCLA of the East" boast, Driesell quipped: "I was kind of drunk or something when I said it. But we were pretty good and we wound up pretty good. We had a lot of great players."
Before Driesell arrived at Maryland, the team was an ACC doormat and had trouble drawing fans to old Cole Field House. After going 13-13 in Driesell's first season, the Terps announced their resurgence on Jan. 9, 1971, with a 31-30 overtime upset of No. 2 South Carolina at home. There was no shot clock then, so Driesell ordered his players to slow the game to a crawl against a team that had defeated Maryland 96-70 just three weeks earlier.
One of Driesell's best teams never made it to the postseason. In the 1974 ACC championship game, the fourth-ranked Terrapins lost in overtime to No. 1 North Carolina State 103-100 during a time when only the conference champion advanced to the NCAA Tournament.
A week later, a Maryland team featuring future NBA starters Tom McMillen, John Lucas and Elmore turned down a bid to the NIT, which it had won two years earlier. N.C. State went on to win the 1974 NCAA title, ending UCLA's seven-year streak as national champions.
"Lefty's team that year," Krzyzewski said, "was probably as good as 20 national champions."
Born on Christmas Day in 1931, Charles Grice Driesell grew up in Norfolk, Virginia. He was a star basketball player for Granby High in Norfolk before attending Duke.
After working at the Ford Motor Co., Driesell took a job as a junior varsity football and basketball coach at Granby in 1954 after convincing his wife, Joyce, that he could withstand the pay cut by also selling encyclopedias. He eventually was promoted to head coach of the varsity team before moving to Newport News High, where he won 57 straight games.
In 1960, he took a job at Davidson, which was coming off an 11th consecutive losing season. He went 9-14 in his debut, one of only two times over an entire season in which he would finish with a losing record as a college coach.
Driesell won three Southern Conference tournaments and five regular-season championships at Davidson over nine years and went 176-65 before being hired at Maryland. He won 348 games with the Terrapins, a long-lasting school record that was finally broken in 2006 by Gary Williams.
Williams won the NCAA title in 2002. When he got home, a note from Driesell was waiting for him. It read: "Gary, YOU have made Maryland the UCLA of the East. Congratulations."
After leaving Maryland, Driesell was hired in 1988 by James Madison, a small Virginia school that finished 10-18 in 1987. He went 16-14 in his first year, 20-11 in his second season and led the Dukes to four straight NIT appearances before going to the NCAA Tournament in 1994.
Driesell compiled a 159-111 record at James Madison and enjoyed continued success at Georgia State. The Panthers were 29-5 in 2000-01 and upset Wisconsin in the opening round of the NCAA Tournament. Two years later, he retired in the early stages of his 41st season with a career record of 786-394. At the time, he ranked fourth in NCAA Division I wins, behind only Dean Smith, Adolph Rupp and Bob Knight.
Finally, at age 71, the man affectionately known by many as the Ol' Left-hander had enough.
"I'm just tired and I've got this bad cold and I'm just going to retire," Driesell said. "I'm looking forward to not having a job. I can get up when I want to and do what I want to."
Driesell is survived by four children. While at Duke, Driesell eloped with Joyce and got married in December 1952. She died in 2021.
The couple's only son, Chuck, played for the Terrapins under his father from 1981-85 and became an assistant to his father at James Madison. He was hired as the coach at The Citadel in 2010 and was fired after five losing seasons.
While helping his father at James Madison, Chuck Driesell learned the rigors of coaching.
"Dad gave me a lot of responsibility, and we worked hard," he said. "As a son and as a player, I'm not sure I understood how hard he worked. I figured it out pretty quickly."

title: Bucs' Tucker Claxton looks to 3rd straight title
author: LUKE BONANNI Special to the Bay Times Record Observer
content:
Bucs' Tucker Claxton looks to 3rd straight title

 February 24, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: LUKE BONANNI Special to the Bay Times Record Observer | Section: News 
 
 445
 Words 

 Read News Document

 STEVENSVILLE — Senior Tucker Claxton has committed to Mount Saint Mary's for the fall. Claxton was a key piece to the 2023 State Championship for Kent Island High School's varsity men's lacrosse team and also contributed to the 2022 team that took home the state prize. This spring Claxton looks to lead the Bucs to a third-straight title.Athletics at KIHS have been very competitive and successful over the last few years. After two amazing years for the Bucs with the 2022 and 2023 graduating classes, Claxton's commitment to the Class of 2024 is unparalleled.
Lacrosse might be Claxton's best sport, but he's also been on varsity football since sophomore year. In 2022, the Bucs were eliminated in the state quarterfinals and looked to bounce back in 2023. That's exactly what they did. Led by Kasey Heath and Claxton, alongside many other key players the Bucs had on their stacked roster, they were able to make the state championship before falling just short to Milford Mill Academy. Claxton stated, "There are a few memories that stick out to me. One was being a part of the first team in Kent Island football history to make the state championship. Another was running out of the tunnel to see a couple thousand people supporting you week in and week out. Breaking the receiving record for Kent Island school history was very cool as well." Claxton broke this record in his final high school game in a quarterfinal loss to Huntingtown. Claxton has also been a member of the varsity basketball team for the last two years.
When asked about playing three sports during his high school career, Claxton said, "I haven't had more than really a week off since Covid. I'm always doing something as soon as one season ends I was right on to another. Even the summer was filled with football camp, workouts, and club lacrosse. But this has taught me great discipline and mental toughness which I think is a hard lesson to find."
Last year, Claxton's role on the Buccaneer lacrosse team increased dramatically. His father, Andy Claxton, holds second place as the all-time leader in face off wins at the University of Maryland, and last season served as the offensive coordinator for Kent Island. The state championship in 2023 meant a lot to Tucker Claxton. "Scoring the game-winning goal in the state semifinals, and winning the state championship with my friends and teammates I've known since kindergarten meant a lot to me. From playing together the whole time, and being able to hug my dad after to celebrate, that was always the dream," he said.
Luke Bonanni is a student reporter from Kent Island High School.

author: Bill Haufe

PLACING THEMSELVES

 February 24, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 773
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — Last Monday's Bayside Conference championships was not one of the more memorable performances by Queen Anne's County High's young girls wrestling program."We didn't wrestle our best," Lions head coach John Waters said.
But Waters used Monday as a learning tool heading into Friday's Class 2A-1A East Regional championships.
"I think with a lot of young wrestlers, not knowing what Baysides mean, Monday was probably the best thing for us because it showed that the girls needed to be focused and ready for every match. A few of them at Baysides won their first match and they weren't ready for the semifinals."
The Lions certainly appeared ready Friday, placing in 11 of the 14 weight classes for a group that now advances to the Class 2A-1A state championships, beginning Thursday at the Show Place Arena in Upper Marlboro.
The top three finishers in each weight class in the four regional girls tournaments advance, where the boys tournaments advance the top four at each weight.
"Overall I'm proud of the girls," said Waters, who had 10 in the championship finals and left with four individual champs. "They really wrestled well. They've worked extremely hard to get where they are. Most of the girls on the team are first-year wrestlers. And if they're not first, they're second. So that says a lot about where they've come. Most of the varsity lineup are freshmen and sophomores."
Among that group, freshman Finley Patchett (125 pounds) and sophomore Bree Conard (115) each managed to win titles after being turned to their backs, as did junior Ally Conley (100).
"That just says a lot about their focus at practice this week," Waters said.
Conley (17-5) scored an early takedown against Parkside's Logan Newton (7-5), got turned, but recovered to earn a pin in 1 minute, 20 seconds to win the 100-pound crown. Conard (14-7) battled off her back and built a 10-4 lead before pinning Parkside's Brylee Davis (15-7) in 4:29 of the 115-pound final.
Then there was Patchett (13-4), who led 7-1 after one period against Stephen Decatur's Rachel Plata (9-2) in the 125-pound final. Patchett was leading 9-2 when Plata escaped, scored a takedown and picked up three near-fall points to close within 9-8 heading into the third. But Patchett, starting off bottom, hit a reversal 17 seconds into the third and added a late takedown for a 13-9 decision.
Junior Keira Corcoran (4-3) gave Queen Anne's a fourth champion when she pinned Decatur's Aya Mejber (2-11) in 3:45 to win the 135-pound championship. Corcoran got a takedown one minute into the match, but Mejber escaped to make it 2-1 entering the second period. Corcoran worked an escape 32 seconds into the second and got a takedown before earning her fall.
"We talked at practice about just being ready, staying focused," Waters said. "And doing what they're best at; not trying to do something they saw on Youtube or something. Just do what you're good at."
Queen Anne's got runner-up finishes from Ava Price (15-6) at 120, Delaney Gray (15-7) at 130, Julia Reburn (11-7) at 140, Lilly Hammond (14-5) at 145, Morgan Morris (5-6) at 170, and Kaylynn Bryant (17-4) at 190. Maggie Rooney (3-7) placed third at 235.
"There were a few matches, especially in the finals, we just came out a little flat," Waters said. "It's hard to come back unless you're ready. But the ones that lost in the finals, they'll have a couple good days of practice, they'll bounce back. They'll be ready. They'll refocus. That's what we're looking for."
Colonel Richardson will have the East's second largest contingent at states, as it qualified eight, led by junior Ryleigh Porter (9-3), who pinned Cambridge-South Dorchester's Sienna Mitchell (9-7) to win the 235-pound weight class.
Colonel's Dale Swann (17-8) lost by fall in the 105-pound final, but four teammates earned pins in the consolation finals.
Luna Infante-Reyes (11-13) pinned Kent County's Rhilynne Ashley-Pinder (4-11) in 4:44 of the 110-pound final. Frankie Aguiar (5-8) earned a 59-second fall over Decatur's Jessica Garcia (1-10) for third place at 120. Landine Dorleans (14-12) defeated James M. Bennett's Sinai Horsey (12-23) via a 2:35 pin at 125. And Olivia McGregor (17-2) wrestled back to earn a 3:46 fall over Queen Anne's Adelina Dickens (8-16) at 1:55.
Colonel's Annabelle Morales (2-11) and Danika Jeanty (4-9) won their consolation finals at 130 and 170, respectively with a bye.
Kent Island went two for two in the championship finals.
Sophomore Lilliana Mellinger (10-1) got a pair of takedowns before pinning Queen Anne's Price in 1:25 to win the 120-pound title. And senior Kendra Coffey (6-2) bundled two first-period takedowns with a second-period escape en route to a 5-2 decision over Queen Anne's Hammond in the 145-pound final.

title: TIME TRIALS
author: Bill Haufe
content:
TIME TRIALS

 February 27, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 1299
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — Giuseppe Mellinger needed a late block.Tremaine Jackson needed an extra minute.
And Scottie Ford. Well, he needed more time than either one of them.
No matter the time frame, Jackson, Ford and Mellinger each finished with the same result Saturday night at Queen Anne's County High, winning their respective weight classes at the Class 2A-1A East Regional wrestling championships.
"He's been one of our elite wrestlers for three years now," Queen Anne's head coach David Stricker said of Jackson, who with his 5-3 overtime victory against Rising Sun's Xzavier Brown in the 126-pound final earned his 99th career win. "Tremaine, he's just so quick. And his power has really come along this year. When he gets in on a leg it's really hard to fend off."
Saturday's region final was the third time Jackson and Brown faced off this season. Brown pieced together an 8-3 decision at the Westminster Duals in late December, then earned a 3-1 overtime win when the two met in the 2A-1A East Regional Duals earlier this month. Their third encounter would also take longer than six minutes.
"They've been wrestling each other since youth, so they've known each other really well," Stricker said. "I'm not surprised it went that far."
A senior, Jackson (35-3) scored a first-period takedown, but Brown escaped with 44 seconds left in the period to make it 2-1 after one. Brown (35-8) rode Jackson through a scoreless second period, and hit a reversal 11 seconds into the third period for a 3-2 lead. Jackson then got an escape off a restart with 15 seconds left in the third to forge a 3-3 tie, sending the match into a 1-minute overtime.
"It's obviously been a bit harder because they've been training him, trying to study my style, his coaches," Jackson said. "They obviously know me very well, the good moves I do. So yeah, it definitely was a lot more difficult than the other times wrestling him."
Brown got in a single-leg shot in the overtime, but Jackson blocked, spun and earned the takedown for the 5-3 sudden victory.
"My last match at the high school, and what was going through my head was, I can't lose," said Jackson, whose second regional title came five days after winning his third Bayside Conference crown. "I feel great. I put in the work. I think I've got a good shot of getting in the state finals."
Ford also had a familiar opponent in his 138-pound final — Parkside junior Rocco Tully — who the Kent County sophomore decisioned 6-0 in the Bayside championship five days earlier.
"I knew it was going to be tougher," said Ford, who coupled two takedowns with a reversal for Monday's 6-0 victory. "Every time you wrestle somebody it feels like it gets tougher and tougher. They always learn from it. I was nervous. I would have much rather faced somebody else I hadn't seen before."
After a scoreless first period, Ford (37-1) hit a switch off bottom for a reversal with 35 seconds left in the second period for a 2-0 lead. Tully (35-9) scored a takedown with 44 seconds to go in the third and rode Ford the rest of the period, forcing overtime.
Neither wrestler scored in the 1-minute overtime. Starting on top, Ford rode Tully through the first 30-second sudden-victory period. Less than two seconds into the second 30-second period, Ford reversed Tully and rode out the remainder of the period on top for the 4-2 win.
"I knew I had a good switch on him because on Monday I had a nice switch," Ford said. "He knows how to throw legs, so he's really tough on top, but I knew I could get out. I just beat him off the whistle."
Something that did not surprise Kent County head coach Chris Yiannakis.
"He's been on that switch," Yiannakis said of Ford. "That's one of his number one escapes from bottom. Most people can't stop it. It's so fast. Rocco did stop it in the first couple of periods though. He just wore him down by the final (period) and he couldn't stop it."
The 175-pound final was yet another Bayside rematch, as Mellinger (36-5) clashed with Parkside's Canaan Mapp (24-8) for the third time this season.
"The first time we wrestled he actually was more aggressive," said Mellinger, who defeated Mapp via a 12-4 major decision during the dual-meet season. "He would actually tie up with me and stuff. So that allowed me to work my offense. The second time, at Baysides (a 7-2 Mellinger win), he would run around, he kept moving, but I got a few takedowns there.
"This time, because I think his coaches were telling him how to make some good adjustments, he wasn't tying up," Mellinger continued. "He was keeping me at a distance. He would try to work in some shots, I would try to work in mine. But we both got a good shot defense. And then when we're so far apart, it's hard to score points."
Mellinger got a double-leg takedown 54 seconds into the match, but Mapp escaped 11 seconds later, making it 2-1 heading into the second. Mapp escaped five seconds into he second period to tie the match.
It remained that way until 18 seconds into the third, when Mellinger, starting on bottom, escaped to take a 3-2 lead. Mellinger blocked a shot midway through the period before a neutral restart with 41 seconds left. Mellinger got in a shot, but Mapp countered with a shot with less than 20 seconds left. The Kent Island senior, who was named the Bayside Conference's defensive player of the year in football for 2023, could not be taken down though, hanging on for the 3-2 win.
"I started getting a little nervous at the end when I took a shot and then he re-shot and got in on my leg with like 15 seconds left," Mellinger said. "And I was able to defend that because if he had gotten that and I didn't get up in time, that would have been the match."
It was Mellinger's first regional title.
"It's nice to win, said Mellinger, whose younger sister Lilliana won the 120-pound title at Friday night's girls 2A-1A East Regional. "My sister and I, we're both Bayside champions. Now, we're both regional champions. Now, we're both competing for a state title. That's cool. It's a lot of fun."
Said Kent Island head coach Tommy Sitar of Mellinger, "He had another great tournament. He worked really well in his matches leading up to the final, and fortunately got the win in the final. It's hard to beat a wrestler three times in a season. It's a good feat."
Kent Island seniors Greg Couch (132) and Cody Sandefer (144) each took runner-up honors, and seniors Brandon Adler (157) and Nick Morey (190) each won their consolation final to place third.
The top four in each weight class advance to this year's state tournament, which begins Thursday at the Show Place Arena in Upper Marlboro and concludes Saturday.
Stephen Decatur and Rising Sun each advanced nine to states, while North Caroline finished with the most wrestlers from a North Bayside school, qualifying six and two alternates.
"We had a rough Monday at Baysides," North Caroline head coach Robin Eaton said. "I preached to them all week 'That wasn't the week to shine. 'Work harder and fix a few things and we could shine at regionals.' And that's what they did. They did everything we worked on; wrestled very smart, wrestled tough. Didn't make mistakes."
North Caroline freshman Caleb Melvin (120), junior Corey Bunce (165) and senior Dakota Kinsey (285) each wrestled-back to win their respective consolation finals, while sophomores Darly Ortega (106), Connor Frank (113), and Jacob Carpenter (126) placed fourth.
Kent County senior Brady Sutton decisioned Harford Vo Tech's Nikolai Chervak in the 144-pound consolation final, and Cambridge-South Dorchester sophomore Mark Jones placed fourth at 285.

title: Harper settling in at first for Phillies
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Harper settling in at first for Phillies

 February 28, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 1090
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Bryce Harper is getting settled in as full-time first baseman for the Philadelphia Phillies.Harper hit a hard single in his first spring training at-bat Wednesday, but the two-time NL MVP also flashed some leather at first base in a 7-7 tie against Atlanta. Harper made a diving catch on Jarred Kelenic's grounder in the first inning, and started nifty 3-6-3 on a 105.3 mph grounder by Kelenic in the third.
"Both of them were real good," Phillies manager Rob Thomson said. "He looks very comfortable and he's improving every day."
Harper had Tommy John surgery in November 2022 and made his season debut last May 2 as a designated hitter. An outfielder the previous 11 seasons, his return to the field July 21 was at first base, where he started 36 times in the regular season and 13 in the playoffs.
"The sky's the limit for me because he's athletic," Thomson said. "He's calm, poised. A lot of a lot of good things can happen."
Former Phillies first baseman Rhys Hoskins tore his left ACL in a spring training game last March, and left in free agency after the season.
MUNCY HITBefore Japanese sensation Yoshinobu Yamamoto threw the first pitch in an impressive spring training debut for the Dodgers against World Series champion Texas, Los Angeles third baseman Max Muncy got hit by a pitch on his left hand in the top of the first inning.
Manager Dave Roberts said the ball hit Muncy on the knuckle of his ring finger and that the veteran was getting tests.
"I'm hopeful that it's not going to be too serious," Roberts said.
After getting hit by left-hander Cody Bradford, Muncy stayed in the game to play defense, and was replaced in the fourth inning by Austin Gauthier before his second at-bat. A mainstay in the middle of the Dodgers order the past six seasons, Muncy hit 36 homers and had 105 RBIs last year.
Yamamoto struck out three batters over two scoreless innings.
COUNSELL VS. BREWERSThere was a mix of cheers and boos when new Chicago Cubs manager Craig Counsell returned to his old spring training home for the first time.
The Cubs won 6-1 on the road Wednesday against the Milwaukee Brewers, the NL Central rival Counsell managed the past nine seasons.
"It's weird seeing him in those colors, but that's what reality is right now," said new Brewers manager Pat Murphy, who was on Counsell's staff the past eight years.
Brewers shortstop Willy Adames went across the field to hug Counsell before the game.
Budget-conscious Milwaukee won three NL Central titles and made five playoff appearances the past six years before Counsell's contract expired. The Cubs lured him away with a five-year contract worth more than $40 million that made him the highest-paid manager the majors.
SONNY OPENERSonny Gray will be the first Cardinals pitcher since Kyle Lohse in 2008 to make his debut for the Cardinals with a start on opening day.
"I don't take that lightly at all," said Gray, the veteran right-hander who signed a $75 million, three-year deal in November. "I appreciate the opportunity and what that shows."
Gray finished second in the AL Cy Young Award voting last season, when he was 8-8 with a 2.79 ERA in 32 starts for Minnesota. The Cardinals also added former All-Stars Kyle Gibson and Lance Lynn to their rotation in free agency.
St. Louis, coming off its first losing season since 2007, opens March 28 on the road against Shohei Ohtani and the Dodgers.
TOP PICK SKENES TO PITCH THURSDAYPittsburgh pitching prospect Paul Skenes, the top pick in last year's amateur draft, is to make his spring training debut on Thursday when the Pirates face Baltimore and Jackson Holliday, the No. 1 selection last summer.
The 21-year-old Skenes had a 5.40 ERA with 10 strikeouts and two walks in 6 2/3 innings in limited action in the minors after signing a record $9.2 million bonus to join Pittsburgh.
While the Pirates have a couple of open spots in their starting rotation, it's likely the hard-throwing Skenes will begin his first full season as a professional in the minors. He was 12-2 with a 1.69 ERA and 209 strikeouts in 122 2/3 innings last spring while playing for national champion LSU.
PEN PROBLEMThe Cleveland Guardians are shutting down reliever Trevor Stephan for three weeks with a deep bruise in his right elbow. Stephan, who appeared in 71 games last season, experienced soreness during a recent training session in Goodyear, Arizona. An MRI revealed the bruising.
Manager Stephen Vogt said Stephan has no structural or ligament issues.
The 28-year-old Stephan went 7-7 with a 4.06 ERA last season.
TJ AGAIN FOR THOMPSONNationals right-hander Mason Thompson will undergo Tommy John surgery for the second time.
Thompson first had the ligament replacement surgery when he was in high school. Now 26 and coming off 51 appearances for the Nationals last season, he felt a pop in his elbow at the start of spring training two weeks ago.
Manager Dave Martinez said Thompson will have the surgery on Friday.
GIANTS INJURIES
Giants right-hander Tristan Beck returned to San Francisco to see doctors after dealing with lingering soreness in his right hander.
"He's kind of been pitching through it a bit," San Francisco manager Bob Melvin said. "It just got to a point where we want to find out exactly what it is."
Beck made his big league debut last season by going 3-3 with a 3.92 ERA in 33 games for the Giants. While he started only three of those games, he is expected to be part of their rotation this year.
Meanwhile, Giants outfielder Mike Yastrzemski made his spring debut Wednesday going 0 for 2 with a walk in their 7-4 loss to Oakland. There are no restrictions at the plate even though he is still building up his throwing from a left shoulder issue that developed during offseason workouts.
SOME CLAIMS AND MOVES
— The Yankees claimed infielder Jahmai Jones off waivers from the Brewers. Infielder Jordan Groshans was designated for assignment to make room on New York's 40-man roster.
— Sam Hilliard is back with Colorado after being claimed the outfielder off waivers from Baltimore. The Rockies cleared a spot on their 40-man roster by putting right-hander Antonio Senzatela on the 60-day injured list.
Hilliard played 214 games with the Rockies from 2019-22 before getting traded to Atlanta. He played 40 games with the Braves last season before Baltimore claimed him off waivers in November.
— San Diego agreed to a minor league contract with 31-year-old outfielder Tim Locastro, who hit .232 with two homers and three RBIs and six stolen bases in 43 games and 67 plate appearances with the New York Mets last year.

title: Perryville outlasts Colonels in region final
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Perryville outlasts Colonels in region final

 March 6, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 666
 Words 

 Read News Document

 PERRYVILLE — After 30 minutes of hard-fought play that featured multiple lead changes, Perryville High's boys basketball team found itself clinging to a three-point lead over Colonel Richardson with 1:45 remaining in Tuesday's Class 1A East Region I final.With a trip to the state tournament on the line, either team could have used a response from one of its players to cement a state berth. The player that answered the call was Perryville junior Devin Clore.
Clore knocked down back-to-back 3-pointers in a span of 40 seconds to extend the Panthers lead to nine with just over a minute remaining before Perryville held off a late Colonel charge to seal a 79-75 victory.
Winning the regional crown brings extra sentiment to this season's Perryville squad, as Clore and several teamates played under head coach Ron Kidd since they were as young as five years old.
"It feels amazing," Clore said. "We've all been playing since we were five or six and we've always had a dream to all come to a high school at one time and just hoop together and that's what we're doing."
After coaching many of his current players for over a decade, Perryville's head coach shared a similar sentiment for the meaning of capturing the region.
"I couldn't be more proud of a group of men in my entire life," Kidd said. "They worked hard every day and hats off to Colonel Richardson. They played us very hard, they were physical and my guys stood up and brought home the banner. I'm very proud of them."
Perryville built a 10-point lead by the end of the first quarter, before Colonel Richardson opened the second quarter on an 8-2 run to cut its deficit to four. Following an eight-point swing that grew the Perryville lead back to 12, Colonel ended the quarter on a 14-4 run, reducing its deficit to a bucket by the break.
After a back-and-forth third quarter saw six lead changes, Perryville went on a 13-2 run for a nine-point advantage by the opening minute of the fourth quarter. Despite Colonel Richardson coming back to cut Perryville's lead to as low as one in the final period, the Panthers used 20 fourth-quarter points from Clore, Sean Beard and Andrew Clark to hold their lead.
Clore led Perryville with 22 points, 18 coming from beyond the arc. Clark followed with 19 points, while Kyle Richards and Beard finished in double figures.
"You've got to stay calm under pressure in order to come out on top so I knew that and I just stuck to that," Beard said. "We've worked super hard all season so it's good to see the results from the work actually show."
Dreden Lake led Colonel Richardson with 23 points, followed by Jazir Dickerson and Makiah Batson, who each finished with 20 points. Colonel head coach Brad Plutschak though foul trouble and lack of defensive execution for a majority of the game led to his team coming up just short. With a young team however, Plutschak hopes the Colonels can use Tuesday's loss as a learning experience.
"We had a little foul trouble and we wanted to press, and we kind of weren't able to until later in the game when we wanted, and it was effective but we just came up a little bit short," Plutschak said. "It's tough but we've got a lot of young guys that will be back and I like their hustle and their effort and we'll just keep building on it."
Perryville will travel to Baltimore as the seven-seed after reseeding to face second-seed Edmondson-Westside in the Class 1A state quarterfinals on Friday. The Red Storm won last year's Class 1A state title. With the first goal of a regional title now behind them, Kidd has high confidence in his team as it moves on toward the state tournament.
"These guys can accomplish anything," Kidd said. "I wouldn't sell them short of any goal. They had this goal to hang a banner on the wall. We've got a regional final, who knows what's next."

title: QA's-Carver playoff cut short by altercation
author: Bill Haufe
content:
QA's-Carver playoff cut short by altercation

 March 9, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 516
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CENTREVILLE — Friday night's Class 2A boys basketball state quarterfinal playoff between Carver Vo-Tech and host Queen Anne's County High was stopped with 6:57 remaining in the third quarter when an altercation broke out between the two teams that left one Queen Anne's player injured.In a press release late Friday night, the Queen Anne's County Office of the Sheriff said, "it was actively investigating an assault that took place Friday on a Queen Anne's County High School basketball player at the game.
"We have obtained and are currently reviewing video surveillance footage as part of our ongoing efforts," the release stated. "No arrests have been made at this time as we continue to review evidence and fully investigate this incident."
Carver was winning 42-15 at halftime and extended that lead to 47-15, when Dorrian Sands hit a baseline jumper and a 3-pointer in the first minute.
Queen Anne's was approaching mid-court on its ensuing possession when a cross-court pass was intercepted by a Carver player, who drove quickly to the basket and was fouled from behind by Thompson. A Carver player confronted Thompson.
Video footage on Twitter showed players from both teams exchanging words near the Carver basket. Players and coaches from both benches came onto the court. The video then shows the altercation escalating when a Queen Anne's player is punched in the face. It is not clear from the video who struck the Queen Anne's player.
Members of the Queen Anne's County sheriff's department, Queen Anne's school administrators and staff, and both coaching staffs quickly separated players. The game's three officials conferred and decided to officially call the game.
"Our players, teams, community and school staff deserve a safe environment, we have zero tolerance for this type of behavior at our public events, and we can assure our community that this investigation will be thoroughly completed, and appropriate charges will be done at the conclusion," Queen Anne's Sheriff Gary Hofmann said in the press release.
Queen Anne's County athletic director Kwandrey Wilson and head basketball coach Jeff Hollis would not comment on the incident.
Carver advances to the semifinals where it will meet Middletown.
As of Saturday afternoon, it was not known if the Maryland Public Secondary Schools Athletic Association would take any action on the incident or dole out any punishment.
Queen Anne's (18-4) took a 2-0 lead on a pair of Vince Gilberto free throws 1:23 into the game. The Bears (16-4) rattled off the next nine points before Collin Woolford hit a 3-pointer for the Lions midway through the first quarter.
Carver, which used a suffocating, in-your face pressure defense, stretched its lead to 16-5 when Sands (game-high 25 points) drained one of his five 3-pointers. Gilberto hit two free throws to get Queen Anne's within 16-7. But with 54.9 seconds left, Gilberto appeared to suffer an ankle injury while driving to the basket and was carried off the court. The senior guard did not return the rest of the game.
The Bears led 18-8 after one quarter, widened their lead to 32-14, then went on a 10-0 run to close the first half, taking a 42-15 lead into the locker room.

title: Late push seals Vikings' title shot
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Late push seals Vikings' title shot

 March 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 691
 Words 

 Read News Document

 SILVER SPRING — Anthony Hughes and Koby Ennals know basketball can be a game of runs.The two juniors were part of the run that mattered most Tuesday night.
A one-time 17-point lead reduced to three, Hughes and Ennals helped fuel a decisive 8-0 fourth-quarter burst that returned momentum back to Cambridge-South Dorchester High's boys basketball team en route to the Vikings earning a 60-53 victory over Fort Hill in a Class 1A state semifinal at Montgomery Blair High School.
Top-seeded Cambridge-SD (24-1) will bid for its first state title since 1996 Friday, when it faces No. 2 seed Edmondson-Westside (22-2) for the Class 1A championship at the University of Maryland's Xfinity Center. Edmondson defeated third-seeded Smithsburg, 79-59, in Tuesday's other 1A semifinal.
"We just got a believe attitude," Cambridge-SD head coach Shawn Tucker said. "We told them, 'If we just slow it down we'll be fine. We just got to be patient.'"
The Vikings went on an 11-1 run to open the game, and packaged a 13-2 scoring spree during the second quarter, when they outscored the Sentinels, 23-8, to carry a 37-20 lead into halftime.
"We turned it over way too much in the first half," Fort Hill head coach Thad Burner said. "I thought that their energy was a lot better than ours, particularly in the second quarter when they extended that lead."
Senior point guard LaShaun Moody (team-high 18 points) had a three-point play and a drive that helped Cambridge-SD build its early 11-1 lead. But Fort Hill (19-4) got 3-pointers from DeShaun Brown (team-high 18 points) and Jabril Daniels (10 points) in the final 3:16 of the first quarter to pull within 14-12 heading into the second quarter.
The Vikings led 16-14 when they pieced together a 9-0 run midway through the second quarter. Ennals (13 points), who scored his 1,000th-career point in the first quarter, converted a Moody dish for a bucket off the glass. Semaj Pinder (nine points) hit a turnaround jumper then scored on a drive. Ennals scored on a put-back before Thomas Wilson canned a 3-pointer for a 27-14 Vikings lead.
Brown hit another trey to end a three-plus minute Fort Hill scoring drought. But Moody hit a 3-pointer, Ennals made two free throws, and Darren Belizare scored on a follow before Moody splashed another trey at the buzzer for a 37-20 Vikings lead.
"We preach getting off to a fast start," Tucker said. "We knew Fort Hill was a second-half team and it was going to be a battle. So to get out on a team like that early is huge."
The Sentinels went on an 11-2 run to start the third quarter, getting within 39-31 with 4:36 to go in the period. Hughes stopped that momentum briefly when he converted a steal into a layup, putting the Vikings back up by 10. A pair of Sterling Perkins free throws moved Cambridge-SD to a 44-33 lead heading into the fourth quarter.
Fort Hill came out bombing in the fourth. Landon Sensabaugh hit back-to-back three-balls and Brown turned a steal into a layup, cutting Cambridge-SD's lead to 45-41 with 6:30 left. Tucker called time and watched Hughes score another big bucket inside to make it a six-point lead.
Jabril Daniels answered with another 3, shaving Fort Hill's deficit to three at 47-44 with 5:38 remaining.
But Cambridge-SD showed it too could respond.
"We just had to come back and be ourself," Hughes said. "It's win or go home."
Hughes scored on a put-back. Ennals converted a pair of free throws. Moody scored on a follow before Ennals snatched a rebound and raced coast-to-coast for a bucket that pushed Cambridge-SD's lead to 55-44 with under 4 minutes to play.
"We made some pretty good runs in the third and the fourth, but (number) two (Ennals) and five (Moody), they were pretty good," Burner said.
The Sentinels wouldn't get any closer than nine the rest of the way, as Moody scored on a drive and made three of four free throws in the final 1:24 to cement the victory and Cambridge-SD's first state final appearance since 1996.
"They're a team that's not going to give up," Ennals said of Fort Hill. "But we're a team that's not going to give up either."
