title: RISE Flag Football aims to build relationships, get Cambridge kids outside
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
RISE Flag Football aims to build relationships, get Cambridge kids outside

 May 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 781
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Since late April, nearly 200 kids, ranging from kindergarteners to eighth graders, have taken to J. Edward Walter Park to throw the pigskin and grab for flags.The RISE Flag Football program — a program run in partnership between the Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy, the Cambridge Police Department, local nonprofit ALL4LOVE, the Boys & Girls Club at Leonards Lane, Dorchester County Recreation and Parks, Under Armour RISE and the Lower Eastern Shore Maryland Criminal Intelligence Network — has been a hit in Cambridge, according to Cambridge Police Captain Antoine Patton.
"The kids are enjoying it," Patton said. "They're loving it. I went grocery shopping yesterday, and I had kids still coming up to me asking me, 'Is it too late to sign up for flag football? We want to play flag football."
With 175 children signed up, the Cambridge league of the national program is at capacity.
On April 27, the league, which is facilitated by the Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy PROTECT Coordinator program, kicked off with an opening ceremony. Patton said there were over 300 people in attendance.
Patton said the program has given Cambridge children something to do on Saturdays.
"We have children who wanted a sport to play between basketball and regular tackle football," he said. "And now we have flag football."
Feedback from parents has also been positive, Patton said. When rain forced a cancelation on May 4, parents told Patton they understood it, but were "so looking forward" to coming out that day.
"It gives the parents time to spend with their children on Saturdays doing something constructive and something positive," he said about the league.
Arinze Ifekauche, deputy director of communications and legislative affairs at the Governor's Office of Crime Prevention and Policy, said in an email that the program has a "profound impact on the community," including promoting youth development, encouraging active lifestyles, fostering community engagement, providing positive role models and instilling community pride.
Patton said they are looking for funding so they can do the league again next year.
"It's a wonderful program," he said. "We're looking forward to continuing it."
When it comes to relationships, Patton said the league gives the kids involved positive interactions with the police. He said CPD officers will be there every Saturday until the season's end on June 15. Two CPD officers are coaching teams, he said.
Cambridge Police Corporal Joe Jones coaches kids in kindergarten through second grade. Their team name is the Bengals.
Jones' favorite part of the program is that it gets kids outside and playing.
"Because this generation, a lot of them like to sit in the house and play video games all day and not go outside," he said. "So at least for 60 minutes, they get to run around and play and have fun."
For his team, and for the parents and community involved, Jones said this program can be a reminder that police officers are people, too.
"They'll see beyond the blue," he said. "They'll see the person, not the uniform."
Ifekauche said the interactions between law enforcement and the community brought on by this program create relationships "built on mutual respect and collaboration."
"These interactions not only promote teamwork and camaraderie on the field, but also contribute to strengthening trust and understanding between law enforcement and the community they serve," Ifekauche said.
MORE THAN A REFEREEAnd the coaches aren't the only role models on the field. High school students in ALL4LOVES's mentoring program come out every Saturday to referee the flag football games, leaving with new perspectives, service leaning hours and a little extra cash in their pockets.
The ALL4LOVE mentoring program, called NextGen, pairs male students at Cambridge-South Dorchester High School with men in the community. Thorpe said the flag football program is a great opportunity for the high schoolers "not only to serve the community, but to just be role models for the younger kids that are playing."
The full impact of this piece of the program may never be known, Thorpe said. But he believes it's making a significant difference.
"Younger elementary-aged students genuinely look up to these high school students as role models, as big brothers," he said. "I believe that that's truly making an impact on these younger kids' lives."
And the younger kids aren't the only ones benefitting from this arrangement. Thorpe said one teen ref came up to him on opening day to tell him how much he loves reffing and how he wants to do it for a career.
"Not only was it serving him in the moment, he was serving the community," Thorpe said.
Thorpe said it's all about the kids and providing opportunities for them.
"We're changing the narrative of what it means to be a kid from Cambridge," he said. "And this is part of that."

title: Bucs survive Easton rally
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Bucs survive Easton rally

 May 14, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 1174
 Words 

 Read News Document

 EASTON — The bus carrying the Kent Island High boys lacrosse team had already left by the time Easton head coach Dennis Keenan emerged from the storage shed that serves as his team's quasi locker room."There's a reason why they're reigning champs," Keenan said of the Buccaneers.
One of the biggest reasons Monday was Kent Island didn't give Drew Schmidt any room or angle to shoot in the dramatic closing seconds, the senior attackman's last shot of his high school career bouncing left of the mark, as the Bucs hung on for a 12-11 victory in the Class 2A East Region I final.
"I thought we played our hearts out," said Keenan, whose team finished the season 11-3. "It was a great game. They're a great team. Coach (Bobby) Woolley does a great job. They'll be a tough out for anybody else."
The two-time defending Class 2A state champion, Kent Island (11-4) is seeded seventh for the state playoffs, and will play at No. 2 Stephen Decatur (12-3) on Wednesday at 7 p.m. in a quarterfinal. The Seahawks defeated the Bucs, 14-11, on April 19 in their one regular-season meeting. Since then Kent Island has won seven straight, including a 20-14 victory over Decatur in the Bayside Conference championship on May 6.
"A little bit more interesting than we would like," said Woolley, whose team held a five-goal lead on Easton with 5:24 remaining in the third quarter. "Two good teams going at it. And there's only one ball and you've got a lot of energy going around. It's tough to maintain full control when a bunch of adolescent boys are getting after it."
Kent Island looked to be in control when Micah Quinn (two goals) snapped a shot over the head of Easton goalie Jack Kilbourne (14 saves) a little past the midway point of the third quarter for an 11-6 Buccaneers' lead.
But the Warriors, despite losing senior midfield standout Hudson Royer to a game-ending leg injury with 7:23 left in the second quarter, began slowly closing that gap.
Senior Tyler Rardin (team-high four goals) rolled right and parked a rocket past Bucs goalie Christian Lemme (nine saves) with 26.3 seconds left in the third to draw Easton within 11-7.
Kilbourne made a huge stop on Owen Wynot (three goals) with Kent Island on an extra-man opportunity early in the fourth. Rardin cranked his second goal into the lower left corner with 9:13 left, trimming the Bucs' lead to 11-8.
Rardin hit the left pipe during an Easton EMO, but Schmidt gain possession and fed Blake Royer for a goal that pulled Easton within two with 8:38 left.
Kent Island, which got outstanding face-off work from Quinn McFaden, who won 18 of 24 draws, won the ensuing face-off but turned the ball over. The Warriors raced down field, and again Schmidt dished to Blake Royer for a goal, bringing Easton within 11-10 with 8 minutes left.
"I definitely got a little nervous," Kent Island senior midfielder Tucker Claxton said. "But we're well conditioned enough to pull it out."
Just 52 seconds after their once five-goal cushion had dwindled to one, the Bucs got back on the board, as Henry Aidan set up Keegan Green (team-high four goals) for a goal and a 12-10 lead.
But Rardin answered. Moving left to right, the senior attackman sliced the Bucs defense and whipped a shot over his left shoulder into the net to make it 12-11 with 6:18 left.
Kilbourne made yet another big stop with just over 5 minutes left, this time foiling Mark Rees (two assists).
"Jack was awesome tonight," Keenan said. "I think we only gave up three goals in the second half."
Still holding its one-goal edge, Kent Island had a chance to kill the majority of the remaining clock, when Easton was hit for a one-minute unnecessary roughness flag with 1:43 left. But the Warriors regained possession on a Bucs turnover.
Easton called time with 1:16 left. Play resumed, with Schmidt holding the ball until both teams were even with 43 seconds left. Schmidt began looking for an opening on the left side. But Kent Island's defense gave him little space and with the Warrior sideline counting down the final seconds, Schmidt fired a shot that Lemme watched bounce wide left to end the game, starting the Buccaneers' celebration.
"I'm super proud of this team," said Hudson Royer, who watched the remainder of the game from the sideline. "I'm super proud of Drew, stepping up as a big part of this team. He's a big part of the reason we were so in this game."
Schmidt and Hudson Royer are both headed to the University of Lynchburg to continue their playing careers.
"I'm just proud of all our guys that stepped up," Schmidt said. "Even when our captain (Royer), one of our best players, went down, we still stepped up and fought back. And we lost by one. We easily could have won that game."
Goals by Claxton and Green staked the Buccaneers to a 2-0 lead a little over 3 minutes into the game. Hudson Royer scored Easton's first goal with 5:31 left in the first quarter, but limped off the field.
Play continued to see-saw. Wynot converted a Gavan Henry feed for a 3-1 led just 6 seconds after Royer's strike. Schmidt and Rardin scored 1:23 apart to forge the game's only tie at 3-all with 2:07 left in the opening quarter.
But Rees scored off a failed Easton clear with 50.8 seconds left in the first quarter, giving Kent Island a lead it never relinquished the rest of the way.
The Bucs outscored Easton, 5-3, in the second quarter on a pair of Wynot goals and one each from Green, Quinn, and Aidan, who scored short-handed midway through the quarter.
"In that first half we executed just how we thought," Claxton said. "We took our foot off the gas a little bit, which looking forward we may try to push out a little bit more. First half executed well. But we had the lead and we were trying to take the time off (in the second half)."
Campbell Taliaferro scored twice in the second quarter for Easton, the second off a Blake Royer assist with just under a minute left in the first half to get the Warriors within 9-6 at the break.
But Kent Island extended its lead to 11-6 on goals from Green and Quinn before Easton's late push.
"I think the game plan was right until they realized the urgency was on their offense," Woolley said. "We played really stout. We made a couple kind of bonehead mistakes that in any game we wouldn't make honestly. And after that we just had to grind out three quarters and finish it out.
"One goal is the margin of victory," Woolley continued. "That's all you need this time of year. It's a full-team effort. I think we did a real nice job with the face-off dot, which helped us get possessions when it mattered. It goes a long way for the cadence of the team. We made some mistakes in the clearing game. But at the end of the day, a win's a win."

title: FINAL PUSH
author: Bill Haufe
content:
FINAL PUSH

 May 25, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports

 Words 

 Read News Document

 COLUMBIA — North Caroline High's Josh Huster said he was coming back, and he was right. He just wished he could have taken his return trip one step further.Easton High's Jake Hershey took a step further than a year ago, but fell shy of his desired destination. And Cooper Baum, Miles Fox, Alexandria Rockwell and Lila Moore went where no player had ever gone before in the history of St. Michaels High's tennis program — the state finals.
That's how the high school tennis season ended for the North Bayside's top hopefuls Saturday during the Class 2A and 1A state championships at the Wilde Lake Tennis Club.
"Not bad for small North Caroline," said Huster, who made his second consecutive state final after last year teaming with Rebecca White to win the Class 2A mixed doubles title, giving North Caroline its first state tennis championship of any kind. "Unfortunately, we didn't win. But I thought we put up a pretty good fight."
During an interview to recap last year's championship run, Huster calmly declared he and Jesse Link would be in states in 2024. Huster backed that claim, as he and Link won the 2A East Region I boys doubles title, then defeated Eastern Tech's Ryan Elmendorf and Lawson Johnson, 6-4, 6-0 in Friday's quarterfinals before ousting Easton's Clay Nagel and Kai Ferraris, 6-4, 6-1 in the semis later in the day.
"We just started slow," Huster said of the quarterfinal and semifinal victories. "And I felt like today we did the same."
But second-seeded Huster and Link could not overcome that slow start as No. 1 seed Jeeva Padmanabhan and William Chen of Poolesville earned a 6-1, 6-2 victory in the final.
"They were a great team," Huster said of the champs. "I don't think they outplayed us. They've probably been playing longer than us; more match experience. We played pretty well together. We only lost twice all season. We were in most every game (today). Credit to them."
Poolesville ended a second North Bayside title bid, when top seed Andy Wu defeated Easton's Hershey, 6-2, 6-0, in the 2A boys singles final.
"He's just a good player," Hershey said of Wu. "I've seen him at tournaments before. He just got the better of me today. He's strong in every aspect of his game. Just a really steady player."
Despite a nasty blister in the middle of his racquet hand, Hershey last week helped Easton win the 2A East Region II title. Third at states a year ago, the Warrior junior extended his undefeated season to 17-0 on Friday, when he beat Hereford's Richard Wang, 6-1, 6-3 in the quarterfinals, then bounced the No. 2 seed, La Plata's King Herald Nacua, 6-4, 7-6 (3) in a rematch of last year's semifinals.
"First match I was pretty happy with," Hershey said. "Couple moments I wanted to take back. And then second match was definitely a grind. Played the same dude I played last year in the semis. Different result this year."
The difference?
"Twenty-hour weeks every single week this summer training," Hershey said. "Traveling all over the Eastern seaboard playing. Really just hours and hours."
But those long hours of work could not carry Hershey past Wu.
"It's not over yet," Hershey said of his high school career. "One more (year)."
St. Michaels had never advanced a player or team to the finals at states until this year, when it had a boys and girls doubles team reach the 1A championship match.
"They have really just done everything that we've asked them to all season long," St. Michaels head coach Jordan Miller said of his two doubles teams. "They have worked their butts off the entire season. Postseason played every match we asked them to and did all the right things. They came out today and they competed. They put it all on the line. They didn't get the results they wanted, but they absolutely showed they belonged to be here."
Baum and Fox didn't drop a game in the boys doubles quarterfinals, routing Patuxent's Brian Platz and Daniel Segar, 6-0, 6-0. The No. 2 seed then defeated Southern Garrett's Ben Nazelrod and Shane Sisler, 6-1, 6-2, before falling 6-3, 6-2 in Saturday's final to top-seeded Arjun Mistry and Hayden Spence of Liberty.
Teammates Rockwell and Moore followed a similar path in the 1A girls doubles bracket. Seeded second, Rockwell and Moore beat Loch Raven's Christine Onananga and Angel Ibeadogbulen, 6-0, 6-4, in Friday's quarterfinal round before earning a 6-3, 6-1 semifinal win over Allegany's Maya Hare and Danica Knight. And though Rockwell and Moore battled, they couldn't beat South Carroll's Caroline Aliftiras and Audrey Lillycrop in the final, losing 6-3, 6-1.
"That's going to be the next step we're going to have to take is our players are going to have to start playing tournaments," Miller said. "That's what we're going toward.
"They were the two seed coming in and held their to final," Miller said of both his doubles teams. "And we're losing one senior. Everybody else is coming back. So we're in a good spot."
Notes: Easton's Nagel and Ferraris lost 6-4, 6-3 to McDonough's Noah Cusack and Chris Jozwick in the consolation match for 2A boys doubles. … Losing in the quarterfinals of the 2A tournament were Queen Anne's Tyler Olah (boys singles), Kent Island's Jamie Tranquill and Queen Anne's Lucy Taylor and Meg Taylor (girls doubles). … Cambridge-South Dorchester's Amy Wanex lost in the 1A girls singles semifinals before falling 7-6 (4), 6-3 to Fort Hill's Jovie Breitfeller in the consolation match. … St. Michaels' Tom Weller lost in the quarterfinals to eventual 1A boys singles champ Hunter Liao of Boonsboro. … Falling in the first round in the 1A brackets were North Dorchester's AJ Fehsenfeld (boys singles), Kent County's Nina Fahrman (girls singles) and North Dorchester's Maddie Tobat and Jules Tobat (girls doubles).

title: A LIFE LIKE FEW OTHERS
author: Bill Haufe
content:
A LIFE LIKE FEW OTHERS

 June 12, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 1588
 Words 

 Read News Document

 The NBA has never confirmed the worst-kept secret in basketball, that Jerry West is the player whose silhouette is depicted in the league's logo.There's probably a reason for that: West never wanted to be the logo.
"I'm just part of the game," West said in a 2021 interview. "I never wanted to be any more than that. I'm extremely fortunate to have had the life that I've had, and that's enough for me."
His was a life like few others: an NBA and Olympic champion as a player, a champion as an executive and someone selected to be enshrined by the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame not once, not twice, but three times. West died on Wednesday at age 86, the Los Angeles Clippers announced.
"We can only hope there is someone we meet during a crucial time in our lives that will change you in ways you could dream about," said Miami Heat President Pat Riley, who played with and worked with West during their time together as Los Angeles Lakers. "Jerry was that person for me."
West, nicknamed "Mr. Clutch" for his late-game exploits as a player, went into the Hall of Fame as a player in 1980 and again as a member of the gold medal-winning 1960 U.S. Olympic Team in 2010. He will be enshrined for a third time later this year as a contributor, and NBA Commissioner Adam Silver called West "one of the greatest executives in sports history."
"He helped build eight championship teams during his tenure in the NBA — a legacy of achievement that mirrors his on-court excellence," Silver said. "And he will be enshrined this October into the Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame as a contributor, becoming the first person ever inducted as both a player and a contributor. I valued my friendship with Jerry and the knowledge he shared with me over many years about basketball and life."
West was "the personification of basketball excellence and a friend to all who knew him," the Clippers said in announcing his death. West's wife, Karen, was by his side when he died, the Clippers said. West worked for the Clippers as a consultant for the last seven years.
He was an All-Star in all 14 of his NBA seasons, a 12-time All-NBA selection, part of the 1972 Lakers team that won a championship, an NBA Finals MVP when the Lakers lost to the Boston Celtics in 1969 — the first year that award was given out, and still the only time it went to a player on the losing team — and was selected as part of the NBA's 75th anniversary team.
"He was absolutely my basketball sage: wise, loyal and so much fun," Clippers owner Steve Ballmer said. "If you were in his presence, you felt his competitiveness and his drive. He cared about everything and everyone. From the first day I met Jerry seven years ago, he inspired me with his intellect, honesty and enthusiasm. He never stopped."
West was general manager of championship teams with the Lakers, helping build the "Showtime" dynasty. He also worked in the front offices of the Memphis Grizzlies, the Golden State Warriors and the Clippers. Among his many highlights as an executive with the Lakers: He drafted Magic Johnson and James Worthy, then brought in Kobe Bryant and Shaquille O'Neal to form a powerhouse title-winning duo.
His basketball life bridged generations: West played with Elgin Baylor, whom he called "the most supportive and the greatest player of that era," and Wilt Chamberlain. As a coach and executive, he worked with a who's-who of NBA stars from the last 40 years: Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, Johnson, Worthy, O'Neal, Bryant, Stephen Curry, Klay Thompson, Kevin Durant, Kawhi Leonard and Paul George among them.
"I marvel at them, at the joy they brought basketball fans all over the world," West said in 2019.
Even in the final years of his life, West was considered basketball royalty. He routinely sat courtside at Summer League games in Las Vegas, often watching many games in a day while greeting long lines of players — LeBron James among them — who would approach to shake his hand.
"The game transcends many things," West said while attending Summer League last year. "The players change, the style of play may change, but the respect that you learn in this game never changes."
James, on social media, offered his condolences: "Will truly miss our convos my dear friend! My thoughts and prayers goes out to your wonderful family! Forever love Jerry! Rest in Paradise my guy!" the NBA's all-time scoring leader wrote Wednesday.
West is 25th on the NBA's all-time scoring list. He knew he was the model for the league's logo — a player dribbling a ball, set against a red-and-blue background — but suggested in recent years that he wouldn't mind if the league changed it.
"While it's never been officially declared that the logo is Jerry West," Silver said in 2021, "it sure looks a lot like him."
West is still the NBA Finals' all-time leader in total points, along with field goals made and attempted as well as free throws made and attempted. He played in the title series nine times with the Lakers; his teams went 1-2 against the New York Knicks, and 0-6 against the Celtics.
"Those damn Celtics," he often said.
West also hit one of the most famed shots in finals history, a 60-footer at the buzzer of Game 3 of the 1970 series between the Knicks and Lakers to force overtime.
Tributes from across the sports world flowed freely Wednesday. The Los Angeles Dodgers released a statement calling West "an indelible figure on the Los Angeles sports landscape for more than 60 years," and the NBA was planning a pregame tribute to West before Game 3 of the NBA Finals between the Celtics and Dallas Mavericks on Wednesday night.
West is survived by sons David, Mark and Michael from his first marriage to Martha Jane Kane, which ended in divorce. He and second wife Karen had two sons, Ryan and Jonnie, who is married to former LGPA Tour star Michelle Wie.
Riley recalled times where, after a Lakers shootaround practice, he and West would head to a nearby drugstore "to eat the best burgers, drink milkshakes and savor a great custard pudding with fresh whipped cream" before going home to nap and get ready for that night's game.
Evidently, burgers, milkshakes and custard worked wonders for West.
"Jerry would kick (butt) in a way that was so skilled and relentless," Riley said. "I was so proud to be there in his presence. I watched, I learned. He made me believe. Being in that aura of greatness was mesmerizing."
Michael Jordan said he considered West "a friend and mentor — like an older brother to me."
"I valued his friendship and knowledge," Jordan said. "I always wished I could have played against him as a competitor, but the more I came to know him, I wish I had been his teammate. I admired his basketball insights and he and I shared many similarities to how we approached the game."
A native of Chelyan, West Virginia, West was known as a tenacious player who was rarely satisfied with his performance. He grew up shooting at a basket nailed to the side of a shed and often shot until his fingers bled. He became the first high school player in state history to score more than 900 points in a season, averaging 32.2 points in leading East Bank High to a state title.
Basketball, he would later reveal, was his therapy.
In his 2011 memoir, "West by West: My Charmed, Tormented Life," West chronicled a lifelong battle with depression. He wrote that his childhood was devoid of love and filled with anger as a result of an abusive father. He often felt worthless, and to combat that, he said he put his energy into playing the game.
West led West Virginia University — where he is still the all-time leader in scoring average — to the NCAA final in 1959, when the Mountaineers lost by one point to California.
"Today is one of the saddest days ever for West Virginia University and the state of West Virginia," Mountaineers athletic director Wren Baker said. "Mountaineer hearts all over the world are broken with the passing of the great Jerry West."
A year after he won Olympic gold in Rome, West joined the Lakers, where he spent his entire pro playing career. He was honored as one of the league's 50 greatest players in 1996 and when the league expanded the polling to 75 players to commemorate its 75th anniversary in 2021, West was selected again.
"You know, it never ceases to amaze me the places you can go in this world chasing a bouncing ball," West said in 2019, when he was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom — the nation's highest civilian honor — by then-President Donald Trump. "My chase began in Chelyan, West Virginia, where I strung a wire basket with no net to the side of a bridge. If your shot didn't go in, the ball rolled down a long bank and you would be chasing it forever. So, you better make it.
"I was a dreamer. My family didn't have much, but we had a clear view of the Appalachian Mountains, and I'd sit alone on our front porch and wonder, 'If I ever make it to the top of that mountain, what will I see on the other side?' Well, I did make it to the other side, and my dreams have come true. I've been able to see the sides, thanks to that bouncing ball."

title: Queen Anne’s County High grad Stewart wins Golden Shoe and Gold Glove honors as part of Wilmington University’s historic season
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Queen Anne’s County High grad Stewart wins Golden Shoe and Gold Glove honors as part of Wilmington University’s historic season

 June 25, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 1519
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Being part of a record-setting team for a second consecutive year was great.Being named to two All-American teams was really cool.
And earning the Golden Shoe Award for leading Division II with the highest stolen-base percentage nationally was pretty special as well.
But becoming the first NCAA Division II Rawlings Gold Glove winner in the history of Wilmington (Del.) University's softball program? Well, that practically knocked over Tristyn Stewart like a high and tight brushback pitch.
"I had no idea that was going to happen," Stewart, a Centreville resident and 2021 Queen Anne's County High graduate, said of the award given to the country's nine best defensive players — one at each position. "The Gold Glove was the last award to come out. I was like, 'OK, I have gotten these accolades. That's cool.' I was very content with where I was. And then the Golden Glove kind of hit me literally in the face.
"I knew that the Golden Shoe was a possibility and the All-American was," Stewart continued. "I did not know that my name was even entered for the Golden Glove. I had no idea that was even a possibility."
But the junior left fielder who helped Wilmington to a school-record 46-16 win-loss slate this season that included a second straight East Super Regional championship and trip to the College World Series, made it a possibility. Stewart chased down drives, made diving grabs, and did not make an error in 103 chances while totaling 96 putouts and seven assists.
"It's awesome that she got the Golden Shoe for stolen bases," Wilmington head coach Mike Shehorn said. "But for her to get the Golden Glove with all the top defensive players that we've had on our team? Last year we had the player of the year in our conference and region. This year we felt like (center fielder) Taylor Gillis was one of the best defensive players we've ever had. And Tristyn just rose to the occasion.
"She threw kids out this year from left field on just absolute dimes, where the other team's coaches just couldn't believe it," Shehorn added. "They were like, 'Where did that come from?'"
Part of it is arm strength.
Stewart and Gillis partnered for pre-game warmups. By the time they had gone through their progression, they were standing on opposite foul lines, throwing rockets back and forth, with Stewart at times launching her final throw over her teammate's head.
"I played football when I was young," Shehorn said. "I was a quarterback and I've always had a pretty good arm. I kept noticing these two throwing the ball from one side of the field all the way across to the other side. And I'm like, 'Man, one of these days I'm going to jump out there and do it with them.'
"So I started doing warmups, and I would partner with them," Shehorn continued. "And I could never throw the ball as far as Tristyn. I'd give it everything I had but I couldn't."
But that strong arm was only part Stewart's defensive success.
"Her arm strength is unbelievable," Shehorn said. "And it's not just the strength of it, but the accuracy. We always say she has a rocket for an arm, and we dare people to try and run on her. Try to tag up and run. Try to score from second because your chances of being thrown out are pretty good because she has an absolute cannon."
While Stewart couldn't pinpoint where exactly her accuracy came from, she acknowledged longevity in the game and all her past coaches were big reasons. She also noted playing catcher as a freshman and sophomore at Chesapeake High was a major factor.
"Having to work in practice on that accuracy 24-7, with throwing down to bases and stuff like that, I was always able to hit my target pretty well while being a catcher," Stewart said. "But now that I'm not utilized behind the plate in college that accuracy is now me throwing to my throwing partners, or to the base."
As for opposing catchers getting the ball to a base before Stewart's arrival on a steal attempt? Good luck.
"To steal more than 30 bases in a season is unbelievable," Shehorn said of Stewart, who swiped 54 bases in 56 attempts, which included a streak of 38. "But to go 50-some and only be thrown out twice it's just. …
"People knew we were going to do it," Shehorn said of running Stewart. "There was no secret. People nowadays have stats and everything so they knew she was stealing. It was just a matter of what pitch. They tried everything. We had teams, they would try and change their defense, would bring an outfielder in and have two infielders around the bag. They would pitchout and for whatever reason they couldn't get her."
Making Stewart's performance on the base paths more impressive was the fact she stole only 19 as a sophomore and was caught eight times.
"Last year I lacked confidence that I was even as fast as I was, which is why I never had as many stolen bases," Stewart said.
High school opponents and fans got to see Stewart's speed her only year playing for Queen Anne's County in 2021 — the 2020 season was canceled due to Covid 19 — when she stole 18 bases and seemingly tracked down everything hit her way in center field. Lions fans also fondly remember how that season ended, with Stewart racing home on Kamryn Brandt's two-out single in the eighth inning to give Queen Anne's a 2-1 victory over Calvert for their first state softball championship.
But Stewart's confidence on the base paths grew steadily this season, especially when she found success against top-flight catchers from top-ranked schools.
"Stealing off of them and sliding in with ease and being safe, it kind of boosted my confidence and my morale to where I was like, 'OK, so I can basically steal on anyone and I'm not getting thrown out,'" Stewart said. "That confidence was just built continuously throughout the season which allowed me to have a lot more success."
Shehorn agreed better competition made Stewart better.
"It's crazy because I had another kid here a few years back, Rosa'Lyn Burton, she was 60 for 60 in stolen bases and was our first Golden Shoe winner (in 2019)," Shehorn said. "I felt like Tristyn had to do it against more mature-type catchers. Not knocking or taking anything away from Burton, but the catchers that we've seen this year have been top level. In fact, going into one of the games in the World Series, one of the catchers was a two-time All-American, and somebody made the comment that they're not probably going to steal a lot of bases against her. I think Tristyn ended up stealing two in that game."
Like her defensive prowess, Stewarts success stealing bases comes from multiple parts.
"For one thing she's very, very competitive," Shehorn said. "It's not just her speed that makes her different. It's her competitiveness. It's her refuse-to-lose mentality. I always say when we play against a team that has an elite-type pitcher, I always like Tristyn to be one of the first to go after her because it seems like the better the pitching, or the bigger the moment, the better she competes."
She's also a quick study.
Stewart led the Wildcats with 81 hits and 57 runs this season, and was second on the team in batting average (.424) and on-base percentage (.455), helping her earn second-team All-American honors on the National Fastpitch Coaches Association team, and third-team honors on the Division II Conference Commissioners Association squad.
She was among Wilmington's first three batters, often batting leadoff. But as soon as the game began and the opposition was going through its warm-up, Stewart was studying.
"She's not just thinking about her at-bat," Shehorn said. "She's thinking about and watching the catcher to see what her release time is like. Who's covering the bag? Are they able to get there in time? What's the pitcher's stride and windmill type so she knows how to get her timing on that.
"I think the other thing is, some kids it takes a couple steps to get going," Shehorn added. "Within two or three steps she's at top speed. Her burst is second to none."
Wilmington defeated Adelphi twice to win its second consecutive Division II East Super Regional title this season. The Wildcats lost 2-1 to Western Washington in their World Series opener, but then bounced back, defeating Augustana, 5-2, to become the first team in any sport in school history to win a national tournament game. The Wildcats' season ended with a 6-4 loss in nine innings to Lenoir-Rhyne.
"You have goals that are achievable if you do certain things," Shehorn said. "And then you have those goals that are kind of far-reached type goals that you would love to get to, you just never know if you're going to. Ever since I've been here, I've always said, my goal was to get to a World Series and have a chance to win one. Year after year we just kept building and building, and getting different pieces to the puzzle added. And she is definitely an important piece."

title: SOARING TO GOLD
author: Bill Haufe
content:
SOARING TO GOLD

 July 13, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 1048
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Aliah Raga has spent a lot of time airborne.She has worked on takeoffs and landings.
She has built speed then soared upwards as if ready to pierce the roof over her head. She has altered those trajectories with suddenness and grace, commanding her 5-foot frame into streamline flips and twists that are a mix between Simone Biles and Peter Pan.
She has come down only to go right back up, launching into a second high-flying, acrobatic arc that preferably ends with both feet planted firmly in one place, as she raises her arms and breaks into a glamorous smile.
Aliah Raga has spent a lot of time honing, polishing and perfecting the components of the double mini trampoline.
A lot of time.
"I've been doing the sport for 11 years," said Raga, formerly of Denton. "It took a lot of practices. A lot of hard days. And a lot of falling."
So when 19-year-old Raga and her United States trampoline and tumbling teammates received late notification about a schedule change on Day 1 of the FIG World Cup in Coimbra, Portugal on July 6, they were left little time to stretch, warm up and mentally prepare prior to their first pass.
Raga was angry.
And that has often proved not to be a good thing for the competition.
"I was actually really angry," Raga said during a phone interview last week. "And for some reason, I don't know why, but I seem to do well when I'm angry, or I feel I have something to prove."
Raga harnessed her anger enough to get through that first day, then came back the following day to post the competition's highest score en route to winning the gold medal in the women's double mini trampoline for her first international championship.
"Definitely," Raga said when asked if she surprised herself. "Honestly, I was just going to land two passes, have fun, and try my best to represent my country."
Fun.
Raga has had a lot of fun since beginning her gymnastics journey at Joan Dyott's Chesapeake Gymnastics in Easton when she was just two years old. She progressed from Dyott's "Tumble Bunnies" to elite status between ages 11 and 12, and eventually outgrew the Easton gym.
Homeschooled, she began making the trek from Denton to the Dulles Gymnastics Academy in Sterling, Virginia three times a week. She continued competing in artistic gymnastics — which includes vault, uneven bars, balance beam and floor exercise — and trampoline. But when she was 12, Raga was diagnosed with osteochondritis dissecans (OCD), a joint disorder in the elbow that can affect young gymnasts. She underwent surgery. When it was discovered the cartilage had become detached in her other elbow she again had surgery.
Despite those operations, Raga came back and qualified in the double mini for the world age group championships in Bulgaria just before her 13th birthday. Soon after, Raga's parents, Adrienne and Will Raga, conferenced with her coaches and decided instead of traveling to Virginia three times a week, Aliah would move in with a host family.
Raga shifted her focus solely to trampoline and tumbling after her elbow surgery. She continued to compete at a high level nationally and internationally, winning the USA Gymnastics championship on the double mini in 2021.
Progress was halted again in January 2023, when Raga tore three ligaments in her ankle during a practice. She avoided surgery, but was in a walking boot for weeks before going into physical therapy. Again she came back strong, winning her second national double mini title — just weeks after graduating from high school — before earning the silver medal at last year's world championships in Birmingham, England.
Raga won her third national championship in four years in Minneapolis last month.
With this being an Olympic year, there is no world championship in double mini, which is not an Olympic event. But Portugal hosted the World Cup, attracting 23 competitors from around the globe.
Then came Day 1's timing snafu.
"We didn't know they moved it up an hour," Raga said of the competition. "So when we went down there to change and get ready and warm up and stretch, (the other gymnasts) were already out on the floor getting their 15-minute warmup.
"So we had no warmup; no stretch," Raga continued. "We only took four turns before we had to salute and compete, which was honestly so stressful. Two of my teammates got injured because of it and couldn't compete their second pass because they were just so stressed."
Raga fumed, and winged her two passes in the preliminaries.
"I just took what I knew and I just did it," she said. "One of them wasn't the correct pass, but it still was enough to get me in the final in sixth place."
The top eight qualified for Sunday's Final 1 competition. And because the competition was broadcast on the Portuguese television, there would be no schedule mix-ups this time.
Each gymnast got one pass in Final 1, with the top four scores moving on to Final 2.
"When you do Final 1 and Final 2, you have to think strategically," Raga said. "Like most people will throw their harder difficulty pass first. But I know most of the girls. Their hardest difficulty is what I call my easier difficulty."
The double mini opens with a strong sprint onto the first small trampoline, where a gymnast launches upward for her first skill or aerial maneuver, lands, then launches into a second skill before a second landing.
On her Final 1 pass — which had a 7.2 degree of difficulty — Raga went through her two skills cleanly and stuck the landing for a score of 25.9, putting her in third place entering Final 2, where scores restart.
Spain's Melania Rodriguez led off Final 2. But the defending world champion, in a bid for the degree-of-difficulty record, over rotated while attempting a triple pike and rolled out on the landing. Portugal's Diana Gaga also went high risk, but couldn't complete her second skill.
Raga followed. She was again worked cleanly through her two skills. And though she took a step on her landing, her 8.4 degree of difficulty proved compensation enough to earn her a first-place mark of 26.8, giving her victory over runner-up Sienna Kuznak of Canada.
"I was nervous, but I prevailed," Raga said. "This is a really big deal for me and I'm very happy it turned out that way."

title: Burnham has new title, old approach
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Burnham has new title, old approach

 July 18, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 800
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Rob Burnham's title has changed, not his approach."I'm competitive to a fault maybe," Burnham said. "I will lose sleep to prepare for a game. I will stress and wake up at three in the morning and go draw stuff on the board; paper, pad at the computer. Watch film and do all those things.
"But I did all those things before I was a head coach," Burnham continued. "So that's not new for me. The only thing that's new for me is there's a fancy title in front of my name."
That title is head football coach at Cambridge-South Dorchester High.
"Super excited," said Burnham, who was announced as the Vikings' new head coach earlier this month. "It's been a long time coming. Excited for the opportunity to be head coach for sure.
"I just like working with kids," the 45-year-old Burnham added. "I like taking a kid and giving him an opportunity to make himself better through athletics."
Though he was a head wrestling coach for two years at William Fleming High in Roanoke, Virginia, this is Burnham's first head coaching job in football.
He succeeds Toby Peer, who coached Cambridge-SD the past three seasons, compiling an 18-14 record, which included reaching last year's Class 1A state semifinals, where the Vikings lost to eventual state champion Fort Hill.
Burnham said Peer has retired from education and is now working for Altec Industries selling trucks.
"I didn't think he'd step away early. But that's what he decided to do," Burnham said of Peer.
Burnham, who has coached high school football for 25 seasons, began working with Peer at William Fleming. When Peer accepted the head coaching job at South Hagerstown he brought Burnham with him as offensive line coach and offensive coordinator. Together they helped the Rebels go 57-25 during Peer's eight years as head coach, and watched running back Isiaha Smith set the state single-season rushing record with 2,918 yards in 2013.
Peer stepped away as head coach at South Hagerstown when he became the school's athletic director. But he returned to the coaching ranks in 2021, when he took over at Cambridge-SD. Again, he brought his offensive line coach and OC with him.
A native of Kalamazoo, Michigan who played left tackle in high school before heading off to Western Michigan University, Burnham will continue handling the offensive and defensive lines despite his new title. He said he isn't sure if he will be offensive coordinator, but knows for certain he wants to run the football.
"We want guys to get out and attack downfield and run the football effectively at every turn," Burnham said. "As an offensive line guy, if I can run the ball every single play and win I'm good with that. Nobody wants to come and watch that, but I'm over it already. If we win the game we win the game. I throw it three times and we win, I'm good with it. I throw it 50 times and we lose I'm not good with it."
Burnham taught eighth grade math for two years at Mace's Lane in Cambridge before accepting a special education position at Cambridge-SD last year.
"Most of the kids in this building I know," Burnham said. "I either had them in class or they knew who I was from being over at Mace's Lane."
The Vikings lost only five players from last year's 9-3 team, including starting quarterback Blake LaBelle, now at Frostburg State University. The fact that the bulk of last year's Class 1A East championship team is back should help, especially on the defensive side, where Burnham plans to change little.
"Defensively, we're probably going to be almost identical because I think our kids played well to the 3-4 scheme with the two high safeties," Burnham said. "Our kids run fast enough to keep everything in front of us. And it's not a bend-but-don't-break philosophy, but it's more of a we're going to give you a little bit and then take away what you try to get, if that makes sense. We run well enough at every position defensively that we're going to be OK."
Cambridge-SD lost four coaches from last year's staff, but Burnham thinks he can handle that transition as well.
"I feel confident in my ability to assemble a staff that can put kids in a place to be successful in most situations," Burnham said. "There's a virtual guarantee that I'll encounter a situation that I haven't encountered before. But I have a number of people that I can call and talk to and get sound advice, people to bounce ideas off of if there's a situation I don't like."
At the top of Burnham's don't-like list is losing.
"I'm a bad loser. My wife said it's not one of my great qualities," Burnham said. "But I'm going to do things very, very similar to the way I've always done before."

title: Going for the gold: Sudlersville Train Station Museum highlights local sports history
author: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com
content:
Going for the gold: Sudlersville Train Station Museum highlights local sports history

 July 30, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: ANDREA GRABENSTEIN agrabenstein@chespub.com | Section: State News 
 
 455
 Words 

 Read News Document

 SUDLERSVILLE — Showcasing a small town with a rich history of esteemed sports, the Sudlersville Betterment Club presented exhibits of local renowned athletes at the Sudlersville Train Museum in July.Sudlersville Community Betterment Club showcased exhibits earlier this month featuring local sports heroes, according to club secretary Ginny Moran.
In addition to baseball Hall of Famer Jimmie Foxx, Sudlersville is also the claim to fame local home for extraordinaire Olympic archers, renowned skeet shooters, award-winning horse racing, championship golf, acclaimed target shooting and historic fox hunting.
Members Alison and Luke Howard, of the Wicomico Hunt Club, spoke on the activities of the only organized fox chase on the Eastern Shore.
The club hunts from Elkton, Maryland, to Bethel, Delaware. The fox chase has a prominent local history as the first fox hounds and foxes were brought to America in Queen Anne's County in 1650, she said.
The Wicomico Hunt Club houses all of their three breeds of hounds together at one kennel near Salisbury, she said.
Sudlersville is also home to several World Class Skeet Shooting Champions including Joseph M. George, who is entered into the Maryland Hall of Fame for Sports for 1,800 lifetime shooting wins. George's grandson, Jonathan Levan, is featured for his accomplishments winning Top Gun at the Grand National Waterfowl Hunt at the age of 17.
Greg Clark from the Sudlersville Skeet Club shared memories from pulling clay targets for the Club as a child.
A display of memorabilia showcased local sports champions Zach Schmidt and David Sink who were National Rifle Shooting Champions at national competitions and went all the way to Junior Olympics. Both participated in the Jacksonville State University Rifle Team in Alabama.
The event recognized former resident Jeff Hopkins for his World Championship of the Archery Shooters Association in 1997. Julie Russum, also from Sudlersville, was a state high school golf champion.
Humans aren't the only impressive athletes to come out of Sudlersville; Slick Tony, a Standardbred Pacer raised right out of Sudlersville was featured having 66 career wins to his credit.
Owner Nola Leager shared Slick Tony's pictures from the Dover, Harrington, and Ocean Downs Race Tracks, as well as recognitions from Hoof Beats Magazine.
Several local equestrians have been big winners in the Trotter and Acer Races and at one time Sudlersville was known as the "racingest town around," according to Moran.
With the mindset of "citizens serving citizens," since 1916, the Sudlersville Betterment Club is a group of volunteers who operate out of the Sudlersville Train Station Museum to collect, preserve, and maintain the history of Sudlersville and the surrounding community.
The Sudlersville Train Station Museum is located at the corner of Main St. and S. Linden St. and will be open during the Peach Festival Aug. 3.
More information about the museum can be found at sudlersvillemuseum.org.

title: Board of Education's vote to resurface tennis courts leaves pickleball players feeling upended
author: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com
content:
Board of Education's vote to resurface tennis courts leaves pickleball players feeling upended

 August 3, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: MAGGIE TROVATO mtrovato@chespub.com | Section: Local News 
 
 677
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — Dozens of Cambridge's pickleball players — some with pickleball paddles in tow — left a Dorchester County Board of Education special meeting on Thursday disappointed and frustrated.Teri Eldenburg, Cambridge Pickleball Club's ambassador to USA Pickleball, said along with frustration and disappointment, she felt shock about the board's decision to approve a project by the James G. Busick Tennis Foundation to resurface the Glasgow Tennis Courts.
"It's a family, and that's going to kill that family," Eldenburg said about the project's effect on Cambridge's pickleball community.
Approval of the project means that the courts will lose the lines drawn for pickleball so only tennis can be played on the courts. This is because a grant from the United States Tennis Association, which the Busick Tennis Foundation has received, does not allow anything other than tennis lines on the courts in the first five years after they are resurfaced.
At the meeting on Thursday, Board Member Chris Wheedleton read a statement with the data points that led him to his decision on the matter. He thanked the pickleball community for their "passion and insights" on the subject.
Wheedleton said the Busick Tennis Foundation has invested more than $315,000 into the Glasgow Tennis Courts since 1992. For this upcoming project, the Busick Tennis Foundation will be contributing $219,000, resulting in a total of $444,000 contributions to the courts, he said.
"Due to this generosity, the county is able to utilize those precious dollars to use for other priorities," Wheedleton said.
Wheedleton also talked about Cambridge-South Dorchester High School's tennis team need for the courts and the potential for state tennis tournaments to be held on the courts.
The Dorchester County Recreation and Parks Department has identified 12 other pickleball courts in the county that the pickleball community can use, Wheedleton said, adding that the department is also working on a plan to build new pickleball courts. He said the department has expressed interest in building those courts on Dorchester County Public Schools property.
"I personally look forward to them bringing that plan forward, adding additional options that can help with all the parties involved," Wheedleton said.
The board unanimously voted to approve the resurfacing project. Board President Sheri Hubbard was not present.
Following the vote, many pickleball players at the meeting walked out. As they left, some residents voiced their frustrations to the board.
"Are you kidding me? We can't even comment?" one person said.
Public comment was not on the agenda for the special meeting, and so there wasn't a designated time for residents to speak. After some residents voiced concern with the lack of that opportunity, Wheedleton said people were able to and did speak at the previous board meeting on July 18.
Eldenburg, who has been playing pickleball for about four years, said in an interview that there are more than 200 people in Cambridge's pickleball community and the courts are used by pickleball players every day. She said the 12 other courts that the county has identified aren't great options because many require a fee and only allow people to play at set times.
Eldenburg, who moved to the area two years ago, said the Cambridge Pickleball Club has given her a family in Cambridge. She mentioned gatherings off the court like Christmas events and meet-ups at RaR.
"Everyone knows your name," she said.
Bill Busick with the Busick Tennis Foundation, who was also at the meeting on Thursday, said after the meeting that he understood the frustrations from the pickleball community, but said the foundation couldn't get the grant from the United States Tennis Association if they draw pickle ball lines.
Busick said the county isn't wealthy, and that is why the foundation raised its own funds to get the courts resurfaced. He said he thinks the pickleball community should organize and raise the money needed for the county to build new pickleball courts.
Eldenburg said she thinks the board's vote will have a significant affect on Cambridge's pickleball community.
"It's going to split us up," she said. "A lot of people are going to go to Easton. People aren't going to know where to play. They're going to stop playing."

title: Davis looks to build on Bucs' success
author: Bill Haufe
content:
Davis looks to build on Bucs' success

 August 23, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 854
 Words 

 Read News Document

 STEVENSVILLE — Zach Davis has always been a builder."I was one of those guys, 'Oh, they went 0-10? Let me give a shot at that thing,'" Davis said. "That was kind of my thing."
As Kent Island High's new head football coach, Davis has been busy building relationships with coaches, players and the community since June. And though he looks to build another winning season, Davis knows he has taken over one of the Bayside Conference's better-built programs.
"I've been a program builder 'til here," Davis said prior to Thursday afternoon's practice. "I really want to see what we can do at a place that's been traditionally pretty good."
After three consecutive three-year stints at schools in West Virginia — Riverside, Nitro and most recently Buckhannon-Upshur — the 39-year-old Davis begins his 10th season as a head coach in a place that hasn't had a losing season since 2006.
"We've been coming to the Shore since 2008," said Davis, whose wife Emily (Gorin) is an Easton High graduate. "We've been trying to come back here. Had a couple of opportunities to come back, but they just didn't feel right. This one felt right.
"The thing about high school football is what works at one program can be different at another program," Davis added. "So when I come here, I have taken a lot of what Kent Island's been good at and just said, 'Hey, let's continue to do that.' My big thing is I try to remember the heartbeat."
Davis continues a family legacy of coaching. His grandfather was a coach, and his father, Storm Davis, who pitched for 13 seasons in the major leagues and was part of the 1983 World Series-winning Baltimore Orioles, coached football at Jacksonville Trinity Christian Academy in Jacksonville, Florida, where Zach was an all-state center.
"I got cut from my middle school baseball team in seventh grade," Zach Davis said. "That was the last time I played baseball. Kind of got to do my own thing."
Davis went to East Carolina before transferring to Liberty University, where he played every offensive line position at one point over three years, and started at left tackle in 2008, his senior year.
"I was in the film room all the time, which prepared me to be a coach," Davis said.
He got into the high school coaching ranks, spending three years at Riverside and three at Nitro before moving onto Buckhannon-Upshur, which is about the size of Kent Island, but played in the state's largest classification against schools from more urban areas like Morgantown and Charleston.
"We always improved it from what it was," Davis said of the programs he coached.
He now becomes only the fourth different head coach in the history of Kent Island's program, succeeding Bryon Sofinowski, who compiled a 118-64 record over 16 seasons (2001-2014, 2022-23), which included leading the Buccaneers to their first and only state championship appearance two years ago. Sofinowski retired after last season.
"I've got coach Sof's keys and I'm going to keep these," Davis said. "It says Sofinowski on it. It's a good reminder where we came from, where we want to go, and how we want to do it."
How the Bucs' new head coach wants to do it is similar to how his predecessor did it, though there may be a few new wrinkles.
"A lot of it is similar but some of the vernacular has changed," said Davis, who plans to keep it on the ground, but likes play action, and also has a two-minute spread package he can use. "Just trying to keep it as similar as possible. If that's what works here, it's good for us.
"As you can imagine, most people are like, 'Who is this guy?'" Davis continued. "I said, 'Guys, I'm here to assimilate into you and then just bring some new ideas. Not that it's better. Some of it's just different."
Senior quarterback Gavan Henry figures to help the transition process, though Kent Island graduated the bulk of its offense from a year ago, including its entire starting offensive line, backs Shane Bogardus and Austin Holland, and top receiving threats Tucker Claxton and Lloyd Price.
The defense also graduated big names, including Bayside Defensive Player of the Year Giuseppe Mellinger. While names will be different, what doesn't figure to change is the unit's base look, which is again under the direction of longtime defensive coordinator Tim Goodrich.
"He tells me all the time if I can score 14 points we'll win a lot of games," Davis said of Goodrich.
As for pressure, Davis said he doesn't feel any added weight taking over a winning program compared to those that struggled before he took the reins.
"I think every good coach should feel pressure," Davis said. "And that should come from yourself, that you're going to do it the best way you can do it. My big thing is win the day. I got that from (current UCLA head coach) Chip Kelly years ago when he was at Oregon. Just be better today than you were yesterday.
"I'm really looking forward to just being here and getting to know everybody, and trying to just keep this program going the way it has been," Davis said.

title: TOUGH ACT TO FOLLOW
author: Bill Haufe
content:
TOUGH ACT TO FOLLOW

 August 30, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 1769
 Words 

 Read News Document

 Queen Anne's County High head field hockey coach Shana Corder already knows there will be no topping last year's near perfect run.All the Lions did in 2023 was win their first Bayside Conference championship in school history, and notch a program record 14 shutouts while yielding just two goals during a magical 15-1 season that ended with a 1-0 loss to Hereford in the Class 2A state semifinals.
"No topping that," Corder said. "The numbers were amazing."
And though Queen Anne's may not be as strong after graduating its entire starting defense from a year ago with the exception of goalie Cassidy Alexander, the Lions aren't likely ready to fall off the map.
"New team, new dream," Corder said. "They know we lost our entire defense, so it's the next man up; fighting for your spots. It's pretty much what we've been telling them. 'Be ready to be a team player. And this might have been your position last year but we need help in this position and you're good here and you're going to go there.'"
Kent Island again looks to be in a position to challenge for its 11th North Bayside title in 14 seasons — excluding the COVID-canceled 2020 championship game.
"It's the most balanced team I've had in my four years as head coach," Kent Island's Laura Harding said.
And should the Bucs stumble, Easton may be in line for its first division crown since 2010.
"This is probably the most athletic group of girls I've had the pleasure of coaching as a whole," Warrior head coach Kim Neff said.
While Kent Island, Easton and Queen Anne's figure to duke it out for top billing in the North Bayside, Debbie McQuaid will look to steer Saints Peter and Paul to a fourth Eastern Shore Independent Athletic Conference championship in five years.
"I'm excited about the energy that the younger kids are bringing," said McQuaid, whose chief conference rival could again be Gunston, which has reached the ESIAC final the past two years. "We've got some versatility so we'll be able to switch lines. That makes the coach happy."
Here's a look at this year's Mid-Shore teams.
EASTON
Head Coach: Kim Neff.
Who's Where: Goalie: Alli Newman (Sr.); Taylor Bowen (Fr.); Defense: Lea Boutte (Sr.); Kadence McGuckin (Jr.); Sammy Townsend (Jr.); Macy Graves (Fr.); Alden Gibbons-Neff (Fr.); Adeline Moore (So.); Midfield: Bis Johnson (Jr.); Myka Motovidlak (Sr.); Addison Knox (So.); Hannah Dahlen (So.); Stella Kabler (Jr.); Forwards: Maedy Leitzer (Sr.); Olivia Orrell (Sr.); Georgia Spies (So.); Ryann Quicke (So.); McKenna Clow (So.); Sutherland Chandler (Fr.).
Outlook: Neff would like to avoid a repeat of a year ago, when the Warriors opened with four consecutive overtime games. She also hopes to find replacements for graduated all-North Bayside first-team picks Emily Branic, Sydney Johnson and Jordan Reagan, but has been encouraged by what she's seen this preseason, which included a play-day win over perennial 1A power Pocomoke.
"This is not a rebuild," said Neff, who returns first-team picks Orrell and McGuckin. "They're just very fast, and they have really good foundational skills. I have high expectations for them, and a lot of them have played together because of travel ball. They really are a cohesive group. We're kind of moving forward from where we left off last year."
KENT COUNTY
Head Coach: Suzie Wright-Taylor.
Who's Where: Goalie: Abigail Strayer (Fr.); Defense: Taylor Strong (So.); Hailey Myers (Jr.); Tess Fuchs (Jr.); Midfield: Abby Gallo (Fr.); Liza Loller (So.); Mali Wirth (Fr.); Forwards: Kate Cannon (Sr.); Grace Gerstung (Jr.); Clare Gerstung (Fr.); McKenna Messik (Jr.); Amaya Spicer (Sr.); Nevaeh Blackiston (Fr.); Mackenzie Walker (Fr.).
Outlook: The Trojans were winless a year ago with one of the smallest teams Wright-Taylor has ever had under her direction, but there have been positive signs this preseason.
"The freshmen that have come in have played rec," said Wright-Taylor, who has often watched players coming through the county's youth program go to other schools. "They have some experience at least, so we're not starting totally from ground zero.
"For the most part that group played together at rec with that goalie," Wright-Taylor said of her six freshmen, which are led by Gallo.
Bolstering hopes are the return of Cannon, Fuchs, Strong, Loller, Grace Gerstung and Messik. And there was Thursday's scrimmage against Bohemia Manor and North East.
"We scored more goals today than we did all last season," Wright-Taylor said.
KENT ISLAND
Head Coach: Laura Harding.
Who's Where: Goalie: Brynja Petursson (So.); Parissa Butler (Jr.); Defense: Sydney Riska (Sr.); Emma Wackowski (Jr.); Laura Peck (Jr.); Kai Moore (So.); Emma Fleshman (Sr.); Makenzie Guidry (Sr.); Midfield: Ella Napier (Jr.); Lilly Snyder (So.); Rita Yost (Jr.); Sadie Latchaw (Sr.); Sydney Cox (Sr.); Lyla Baily (Jr.); Caelan Green (Jr.); Elizabeth Talbott (Sr.); Forwards: Ellie Burnside (Sr.); Audrey Fleshman (So.); Caroline Levin (Sr.); Willow Yost (Jr.); Parker Tengwall (So.); Anna Fronczek (Jr.); Madison Jordan (Sr.).
Outlook: The Bucs went 8-6 a year ago, which included three straight one-goal losses to open the season and another against Queen Anne's in the 2A East Regional playoffs that ended it.
But Harding is excited by what she has seen this preseason.
"I don't have like a Megan Carpenter," Harding said of her former standout now playing at the University of Massachusetts. "I just have a full squad of girls that play field hockey year round. It's fun to watch."
The return of Riska, who did not play last year, strengthens the defense, while Burnside and the Yosts — all first-team North Bayside picks — provide a solid foundation which could be set for a series of title challenges.
"Talent across the board," Harding said. "I think we have a lot of depth. The kids coming off the bench are almost as strong as the kids starting on the field."
NORTH CAROLINE
Head Coach: Molly Elliott.
Who's Where: Goalie: Selena Lopez (Jr.); Alyssa Hand (Fr.); Defense: Brooklyn Spencer (Jr.); Abby Jones (Jr.); Emily Kimble (Sr.); Midfield: Morgan Knott (Sr.); Kylie Ogden (Jr.); Ashlynn Bisesi (So.); Reece Bisesi (Jr.); Forwards: Gracie Faulkner (Jr.); Jamie Robey (Fr.); Julia White (Fr.); Reagan Rizer (Jr.).
Outlook: After five years as Easton's junior varsity head coach, Elliott begins her third year with the Bulldogs, the last two as head coach.
And though North Caroline doesn't figure to challenge for a division title, Elliott has three players with club experience, including Knott, who has verbally committed to play at Central Michigan.
"We have a lot more experience on the field than we have had in seasons past," Elliott said. "We've been plagued the last few seasons by some major injuries So having Morgan and Ashlynn and Reece on the field at the same time isn't something we've been able to do in seasons past, and so I'm very excited that we have a very healthy starting midfield line.
QUEEN ANNE'S
Head Coach: Shana Corder.
Who's Where: Goalie: Cassidy Alexander (Sr.); Caroline Kimball (Jr.); Defense: Melanie Gill (Fr.); Midfield: Ava Fields (Sr.); Ellee McLean (Sr.); Haley Cole (Jr.); Jordan Bilbo (Jr.); Taylor Brown (So.); Ella Rebstock (So.); Forwards: Aly Edwards (Sr.); Jolie Leager (Sr.); Jamie Baldwin (Sr.).
Outlook: Like a number of coaches, Corder will shift players between lines, especially at midfield and forward.
But whereas the defense was last year's anchor, this season it will be the offense that needs to shoulder the load
"My defense carried us last year," said Corder, whose team didn't yield a goal until the final regular-season game against Stephen Decatur. "This year my message is offense needs to do the same until they can figure out their way and our strategy on defense."
While Corder is mixing a new lineup to replace first-team all-North defenders Abbie Denes — now at St. Mary's — Julia Reburn and Molly Holthaus, and well as North Bayside player of the year Faith Novak and first-team forward Gabrielle Scully, there is talent up front.
Corder said she will lean on Cole, who is headed to James Madison at the midfield. Bilbo, who had a knack for big goals a year ago, is also back. Fields and McLean have started four years, giving Queen Anne's one of the strongest midfields in the Bayside.
"It's going to be a different year this year for Queen Anne's field hockey," Corder said. "We're going to rebuild, but it's totally fine."
ST. MICHAELS
Head Coach: Karen Hopkins.
Who's Where: Goalie: Olivia Patrick (Jr.); Defense: Brynn Lizewski (Sr.); Phoebe Cole (Sr.); Regan Wibberley (Jr.); Rebeca Martinez (Jr.); Midfield: Jordyn Beckett (So.); Stella Wibberley (Fr.); Kim Montoya-Guzman (Fr.); Midfield: Molly Genrich (Sr.); Maddie Dunker (Sr.); Tess Weller (Jr.); Forwards: Karina Mazur (Sr.); Abbie Fisher (So.); Ella Marr (Fr.); Penny Turner (Fr.); Zoe Cerrato (Fr.); Kayla Montoya-Guzman (Jr.).
Outlook: Returning first-team midfielders Dunker and Genrich, and forward Mazur give the Saints a nice base to work off. The defense returns plenty of experience, and generating more offense will be among the top priorities.
"The leadership we have through our five seniors is very apparent," Hopkins said. "They've been helping the younger girls as well as leveling up their play. We have such positive energy on the field. We're striving for the intensity. We are striving for better plays and more strategy and more consistency."
SAINTS PETER & PAUL
Head Coach: Debbie McQuaid.
Who's Where: Goalie: Pyper Mister (Fr.); Rynn Morgan (So.); Defense: Kat Murphy (Sr.); Reagan Wolters (Fr.); McKenzie Foster (So.); Lucy Rankin (Jr.); Midfield: Claire Beiber (Sr.); Sadie Jacobs (Fr.); Angie Webb (So.); Forwards: Jules Stepp (Jr.); CC O'Connor (Sr.).
Outlook: The Sabres lost a number of key players from last year's 14-2 title-winning team, including ESIAC player of the year Gennie Webb — now at Virginia Commonwealth — Morgan Quade, Emmary Sweeney, Cadence Kelley and Schuyler Gary.
The cupboard is hardly bare though.
Angie Webb returns at the midfield and is joined by St. Michaels transfer Beiber, who is headed to VCU. The front line also looks strong with Stepp and O'Connor returning.
"I usually get some really good athletes, but they're not always field hockey players," McQuaid said. "This year I've got a good bunch of athletes who are actually field hockey players."
GUNSTON
Head Coach: Yvonne Gazelle.
Who's Where: Goalie: Lorelei DeGour (Fr.); Defense: Izzy Labrador (Fr.); Victoria MacGlashan (Sr.); Lila McDermott (Fr.); Midfield: Layla Kent (Jr.); Genevieve Baughman (Jr.); Camilla Nonemaker (So.); Forwards: Grace Shepherd (Sr.); Gabi Shepherd (So.); Kate Zottarelli (So.); Tori Nessly (Sr.).
Outlook: Sophia Kent, a four-year fixture in goal, has graduated and is now at St. Mary's. The Herons have made it to the ESIAC championship the past two years, but Gazelle thinks it will be a year of trying to find the right combinations in hopes of making a third straight conference final.
"It's going to be a building year," Gazelle said. "We're all pretty new. We have some brand new ones to the sport, but there's a lot of promise."
Layla Kent provides a building block at midfield, while Grace Shepherd figures to be a force up front.

title: WELL GROUNDED
author: Bill Haufe
content:
WELL GROUNDED

 September 4, 2024 | Star Democrat, The (Easton, MD)

 Author/Byline: Bill Haufe | Section: Sports 
 
 866
 Words 

 Read News Document

 CAMBRIDGE — He's been running offenses for 20 years, including the last four seasons at Cambridge-South Dorchester High.But Rob Burnham, who took over as Vikings head coach in July, knows a thing or two about defense.
"For the last 13 years I've just been an offensive guy," said Burnham, who during that span was an assistant to former Vikings head coach Toby Peer, first at South Hagerstown, then at Cambridge-SD. "But I've coached defense previously for a dozen years so it's not new. Just having to oversee everything is a little bit different. But I like doing it."
Burnham has liked what he's seen on both sides of the ball this preseason from a team that returns 18 starters from last year's 9-3 Class 1A East Region championship outfit that reached the state semifinals, where it lost to eventual state champ Fort Hill.
The graduation of Class 1A first-team all-state quarterback Blake LaBelle — now at Frostburg State University — may affect the passing game, but Burnham thinks 6-foot-2, 190-pound senior Anthony Hughes can run the offense just fine.
"We lose the all-state quarterback and that stings a little bit," Burnham said. "But we can find other ways to make up for the great things he did for us, and do the best that we can with the kids that we have and find a way to make them successful.
"We don't have an all-state quarterback this year I don't believe, unless he just cranks it up and starts throwing it a whole lot better," Burnham said of Hughes, who is backed up by freshman Nate Twilley (5-11, 200). "But Anthony's strength is not his arm, it's his legs. He has the ability to throw, but he's a better runner than he is a thrower."
The Vikings could again have one of the Bayside Conference's better running attacks, led by returning starter Sterling Perkins, a 5-8, 180-pound junior, who along with Hughes helped the Vikings reach the Class 1A state basketball championship game back in March. Senior Will Jackson (5-10, 170) and juniors Ra'Qwan Cornish (5-11, 150) and Jayden Hollowel (5-10, 175) all have the potential to bust the big play every time they touch the ball.
"I think our run game is certainly going to drive the bus," Burnham said.
Covering Cambridge-SD's fleet of receivers could drive opposing defensive coordinators crazy. Heading that cast is senior Antonio Blueford (6-4, 190), a four-year starter, and junior Magestic Jones (5-11, 180) a three-year returning starter. They are joined by juniors Tamyron Evans (5-10, 160), TJ Wilson (6-2, 175) and Leonbre Chester (6-1, 180), and senior Kimir Lake (6-0, 160).
"We've got some kids that run fast and jump high," Burnham said. "The plan is to try to find the best things that we can execute and get the ball in our playmakers' hands in space and let them do their thing. We try to maximize their ability."
Senior left guard Omarian Travers (6-4, 255) is the lone returning starter on the offensive line. He starts between freshman center Telorian Williams Jr. (6-4, 265) and sophomore left tackle K'Marion Hall (6-2, 240). The right side of the line has sophomore Jeffrey Sellman (5-11, 240) at guard and junior Russell Johnson (6-2, 200) at tackle. Senior KaMarii Stanley (6-2, 190), who's been on varsity all four years, is at tight end.
"I think we've done well up front blocking," Burnham said. "We've had a tremendous amount of improvement that we've done over the course of the last year or so in offensive line play. Our group of kids that we have are picking up things pretty quickly, and I think we did well with our run game."
Cambridge-SD has done a solid job against the run in preseason, with sophomore JaKuez Sneed (5-9, 210) starting at nose guard flanked by senior tackles Jairyn Lewis (6-2, 195) and Stanley.
The tall, rangy Blueford has the potential to be a wrecking machine at outside linebacker, a unit that includes Hughes, Wilson and Chester. Senior Christen Dockins (5-11, 175), who led the team in tackles a year ago, returns at inside linebacker, teaming with senior Donnell Cephas (5-10, 190), Perkins and Hollowell.
"Defense will be the backbone of our team," Burnham said. "We're pretty stout against the run and we're fast everywhere. I don't want to sound conceited, but we don't have slow kids on defense. Every position is fast."
That's especially true in the secondary where Lake will start at corner with either Jones or Cornish, while Jackson and Evans start as safeties.
"I've been pretty impressed by our ability to tackle," Burnham said. "We've only missed a handful of open-field tackles in our scrimmages but we've had a couple of mishaps in coverage. But it's to be expected when you go out and scrimmage. You try to teach from that stuff. It's a learning experience, and you get better and you don't make that mistake again. If we get good film and we teach from it the scrimmage is successful."
Junior Collin Bair handles the kicking duties.
"I can't wait to get on the field Friday night and see what our kids can do," said Burnham of the Vikings' season opener at North Caroline. "And I think our kids are excited too. That's ultimately the important part."
